I
should like to follow up the remarks already made by the other British Columbia members on the fisheries department's general estimates. Before doing so, however, like my other colleagues, I should like to congratulate most heartily the hon. member for New Westminster upon his thorough and searching analysis of our position as to fishing on the continental shelf, both on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. It is an. analysis which should be studied closely not only by the Minister of Fisheries but also by the minister of external affairs.
We have had a fine example of international cooperation on this continent. We are proud of our long undefended international boundary. Of all forms of international cooperation I think the cooperation between the Americans and the Canadians in the Pacific fisheries reaches a high which should be worthy of emulation by any other country in the world. There is no antagonism at all. We have pooled our resources; we have set up these international joint commissions to control both sockeye and halibut fishing. The Americans have spent a lot of money in Canada building up fisheries which will be used both by themselves and by Canadians. Certainly this is true on the Pacific coast of fish which spawn either in Canada or in the United States or in offshore waters. To us in British Columbia it seems a most unfortunate situation that the United States and Canada cooperate to conserve the fish, to encourage the propagation of fish, and then countries like Russia and Japan on the Pacific and Spain and Portugal on the Atlantic are allowed to come in and plunder them by ruthless fishing on the continental shelf. I suggest to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that he should study the speech of the hon. member for New Westminster, especially that part of it in which he suggests that since the United States and Mexico have proclaimed the continental shelf of United States and Mexico, American and Mexican territory, we should be considering the same thing in Canada.
I should like to say a word or two about the excellent work the fisheries department is

doing, and especially to commend the minister for his announced plan of increasing his staff by at least one hundred young fishery recruits. Excellent work has been done in British Columbia by his research staff. They have been exceptionally good in advising the fishermen and the industry in regard to the processing of fish and in the use of fish. They have not been perhaps quite as helpful in their biological studies. There is still too much about western fish that neither the fishermen nor the industry really understand. May I give one example? It is that of the new anchovy fishing, which is being done for the first time on the west coast this year. I am especially interested in anchovy fishing, because the two canneries which pack them are in my own riding. But where the anchovies come from and where they go is entirely unknown to the fisheries department and the fishermen themselves. Therefore in the process of expansion of his department I urge the minister to make a more generous contribution toward the expansion of the biological division of his research department.
I should now like to offer just one word of criticism of certain methods of the fisheries department. I am glad the Minister of Justice is in his place, because it involves him perhaps more than it does the Minister of Fisheries. During this session we have heard a great deal on the invasion of the rights of British subjects, particularly with regard to the espionage trials. I have been thinking that some of our west coast fishermen are treated much worse in so far as their rights are concerned in the matter of trials than were the people who appeared before the royal commission on espionsife. Let me explain what I mean by that. Up in the north end of my riding there is a very large fishing ground called Rivers inlet. In the area there are regulations which say, for example, that a fisherman must fish within certain boundaries. In areas where strong tides run or where there are high winds the fishermen on occasions may drift over the boundary. Quite often the fisheries department allege he has drifted over the boundary, and the fisheries inspector or guard who arrests that man does not take him before an ordinary magistrate or judge and charge him with an offence. He is brought before the fisheries supervisor who is put there by the fisheries department, and he is told that he can be tried right there or his gear will be confiscated and his licence removed until he can be tried in the fall before a regular magistrate. Just think of the position of a man who is three hundred miles away from the nearest magistrate. He is told that he can

Supply-Fisheries
plead guilty, and be fined $50 or $100 and that he can go back fishing the next morning, otherwise he must wait until the fall but in the meantime he cannot fish, although it is the height of the fishing season. In these circumstances you can well understand what the fisherman will do. He pleads guilty, even though innocent, because it is cheapest. The best example of that is the record of fisheries prosecutions in the Rivers inlet area. I doubt very much whether more than one or two have pleaded not guilty before the fisheries supervisors in the past two or three years. Fishermen would far rather plead guilty, pay the $100 fine and get back to fishing the next day, than wait till the fall to be tried in Vancouver or some other place, and in the interval be stopped from fishing. May I give an example of how it would affect prairie members if the same thing happened in their section of the country. If you grew a little grain just outside the boundary of your farm, the local policeman would come along and arrest you and would take you to the chief of police, not to a judge. The chief of police would say, "You can plead guilty now and pay a fine of $50 or $100; otherwise I will take away your harvesting equipment from you; I will not allow you to harvest your crop until all the other farmers have harvested theirs; and then often your crop is destroyed. You can appear before a magistrate in your community and have an ordinary trial." That is the condition which the fishermen have accepted up until now. The time has come when we should have a circulating magistrate removed from the fisheries department to administer proper justice. I submit it is not fair that these fishery supervisors should be conducting summary trials. The situation is not grave near Vancouver, because there are magistrates in that city, but in the north end of my own riding and in the riding of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, where some of the principal fisheries of British Columbia are located, that is the situation, and it is not good enough. When the minister comments later I should like him to touch on this subject of summary trials by fisheries supervisors.
Members from eastern Canada may have been a little puzzled to-day to see members from British Columbia disagreeing with each other. Generally we all present a united front, but to-day the hon. member for Comox-Alberni disagreed with the suggestions of the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Fraser Valley with regard to gill netters. When the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member 63260-350J
for New Westminster speak a little later I am sure that they will offer rebuttal. The answer, of course, is that in the riding of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni the fishermen are chiefly seine fishermen; in the other areas they are almost entirely gill netters. To those who are not familiar with fishing may I say that there are just three principal methods of fishing for salmon on the west coast. There is the small boat which has a gill net perhaps a hundred yards long. The net is laid out from the boat and the salmon run into it and are caught by the gills. Obviously that fishing must be done at night, or, in the alternative, in muddy waters, because otherwise the salmon see the net and avoid it. A much better way of fishing is to find a school of salmon, lay a long net around the school, pull the bottom tight, forming a purse, and lift the salmon out. That is seining. Finally, the best way of catching salmon is undoubtedly the fish trap, where a large fixed trap is built out from the shore, and as the salmon come from the sea along the shore they go into the trap. Undoubtedly the trap provides the least employment in terms of men. The gill net provides the most employment, but we must think not so much in terms of what fishing will supply in terms of employment, but of which is most efficient in view of conditions five or ten years from now, when we shall have to compete on the world market with Russian and Japanese salmon, because the Russians will use traps, not gill nets.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has said, the Americans catch their half of the Fraser river salmon with seines. The situation is exactly as though, to refer to the prairie provinces, there were a law in Saskatchewan forbidding the use of combines to cut wheat, and requiring that all wheat be cut with a hand sickle and threshing be done by oxen, as in biblical times, in order to provide more work. That is all right if you have a closed economy, but if British Columbia is to compete again on open world markets, as we had to do in the years before the war, we must fish economically. I suggest that the time has come for the departmental officials to give leadership to the fishermen and point out that salmon fishing, which has been so wonderful during the war years in the way of returns, because we could sell every can of salmon we produced, is going to compete in the post-war years with the same Pacific salmon caught by Russia and Japan, and that these gill netters should start to do as all American gill netters did years ago, and turn their thoughts to seining Aside from that I do not propose to enter into the controversy
Supply-Fisheries

between the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for New Westminster as to the relative values of gill netting and seining.
I should be glad if the minister would give in his reply some indication that fishermen fishing in the rivers off the west coast of Vancouver island should have the right to plead not guilty to an infraction of fisheries regulations and be tried by their magistrates without their gear being impounded and their licences removed until they are found guilty or not guilty.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I am in a rather embarrassing position. To-day I have to follow and disagree with two of my colleagues from British Columbia who happen to be my closest personal friends. I have one advantage they do not have-or maybe it is a disadvantage. For reasons known only to myself they had to make good speeches today. I do not have to.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: You could not.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
The hon. member is unkind to me; he says I could not, but I will not show him up by making one of my usual good speeches, only a normal one, which will still be better than his. When he told us about the anchovies, I wondered if any hon. member had ever seen an anchovy. It is a baby sardine, and a baby sardine, as I understand it, is a baby salmon. Incidentally, for the benefit of some of my hon. friends I am not an expert on fisheries. I have had more interesting things to do than to watch the love life of anchovies; I do not know whether they have love nests or not. But I have had a few samples of the finest salmon in the world sent to me from British Columbia. Whether I was being lobbied or not I do not know. By the way, speaking to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I have some chickens on my farm for which I would welcome some wheat from Saskatchewan. So far the maritimes have not sent me any tins of lobsters; I am still waiting, and I should be glad to receive them.
The hon. member for New Westminster is the greatest authority in this House of Commons on fish, and he will speak in detail on my behalf, as to why the hon. member for New AVestminster and the hon. member for Fraser Valley are opposing the use of the seine in favour of the gill net.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Would you know yourself?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I did not interrupt the hon. member for Vancouver North, because I wanted to give him every chance in the world to try to make a good speech. And as the hon. member for Temiscouata is not here to advise me to-day, I hope the hon. member for Vancouver North will help me by not interrupting. I am going to give some of the reasons why I am opposed to the use of seines and am in favour of gill nets.
One of the most practical reasons is something which members of all parties will appreciate, in spite of the fact that they may deny it: we are all interested in votes. We are accused of talking politics. All right; frankly I am talking politics.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Do you use gill nets for that?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I would use gill nets or anything else. One reason I received one hundred per cent of the fishermen's votes in my riding is that I have been fighting for the fishermen, not for the canners. And one reason I am in favour of gill netting is that we have more employment through gill netting. Ninety-nine per cent of the seine boats are owned by the big canning interests. One hundred per cent of the gill nets are owned by individual fishermen. The average gill net boat with net costs SI,500 to S2,000. I do not know what a seine net boat costs, but is is a much larger amount of money. To the best of my ability I am attempting to support the gill netters of my riding, and I have many hundreds resident there, although they do not necessarily fish there all the time. One hundred per cent own nets, and ninety per cent are veterans of this or the last war. We recognized as a government that we should encourage these men; under the Veterans Land Act we enable them to borrow the capital needed to go into the business. Therefore why we should by any manner of means detract from their opportunity to earn a living I cannot understand.
There is a very appropriate name for Vancouver North, given to a place which happens to be situated in my riding. The life or death of the salmon business on the whole Pacific coast depends on a district which, as I have said, has a name far more appropriate to some point in Vancouver North or Comox-Alberni: It is "Hell's Gate." But for the improvements [DOT]which the international commission of which the hon. member for New AVestminster is a member put in at this gate-

Supply-Fisheries
way, you would have no salmon fisheries in British Columbia or on the Pacific coast. Hell's Gate happens to be situated in my riding.
The salmon industry works with the seiners. Admittedly if you put in a seiner you take all the fish out, whether edible fish or not; that net gathers in all the fish which happen to be in that particular area. As I understand it, although I am ready to be corrected, the only net which allows for selective fishing is the gill net. That is the second reason I am particularly interested in it. I would point out to hon. members, and again I am speaking from memory, that prior to 1913, I think it was, we had the slide at Hell's Gate caused by the Canadian National, and had it not been removed, the revenue to the people of Canada from the salmon industry of British Columbia would have been much less than $41,000,000. We went to all this trouble and expense internationally to remove the slide in order that the fish might come to their little love nests in Adam river and elsewhere. Why should we now, by any legislative act, curb the operations of the gill netters? I will leave it to the hon. member for New Westminster to enlarge on this matter on my behalf, as he is more familiar with it. After all, what we are interested in is to obtain enough fish for our food and a fair share of the external market on an international basis with the United States, without worrying about the seiners.
I have no particular quarrel with the canning industry. But these gill netters, according to the figures given us by the international fisheries commission, are quite capable of looking after the present cycle of fishing. I want to be fair about it. One of the unions in my own riding has wired and written me asking me to change my stand. Again I am like the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the only difference being that he has never given that advice to his union. They will have to show a much stronger reason than they have shown thus far before I will make any change in my opinion.
So far as the Fraser Valley riding is concerned, we are definitely and unalterably opposed to the use of seine fishing at the mouth of the Fraser river, and we are definitely opposed to any alteration in the report of the Sloan commission. The Sloan commission was credited with making the finest report ever brought in with respect to fisheries on the Pacific coast. The author of that report was also asked to make one with respect to reforestation, and he was thought of so highly that he was asked to advise with respect to labour legislation in western Canada. In the Fraser
river valley I can see no reason as yet why his recommendation should be altered in any shape or form.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate that consideration of a subject, as important as this has been left until the tail end of the session. I must say in fairness, however, that it is not the fault of the Minister of Fisheries, because for at least the past two weeks he has been prepared to bring his estimates before the house, although they were reached only yesterday.
First of all, before asking the minister one or two questions I have in mind, I should like to reply briefly to some of the statements made by the hon. members for Comox-Alberni and Vancouver North. To-day history repeats itself in the House of Commons. I am reminded of the old seine and gill net fight which took place in the house when I came in the early thirties. I need not repeat the facts respecting the three types of fishing mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver North. However, the seine boats which are spoken of to-day were not allowed in those areas from the days of confederation until about 1933. The argument put forward by the seine boats in those days was that the variety of fish caught-not the sockeye salmon, but a variety of fish known as the pink salmon-had better value if they were caught out in the open water where the American seiners were fishing, or in close proximity thereto. So in the year 1933, for one variety of salmon only-not for the sockeye but for the pink salmon-those seine fishing boats were allowed into the gulf of Georgia. I predicted, and it has come true, that if the seine boats were ever allowed to go into those areas in the gulf of Georgia they would not stop at fishing for pinks, but they would want to get sockeye and all other varieties as well.
The fight was carried on here in the House of Commons year after year. Each year when the estimates came up we battled it out, until the matter was placed before the fisheries committee. There the battle was continued. Entering also into the picture in those days was the matter of traps. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver North, there are three types of fishing-trap fishing, seine fishing and gill netting. If you want to get the best quality of fish and to get it in the cheapest way, you do it by traps. But everyone who is looking toward the giving of employment will, for more than one reason,, be in favour of allowing fishermen to catch their fish by gill nets.
In answer to one of the arguments put forward to-day, even if one catches fish with
Supply-Fisheries

seines he is not cheapening the cost of the fish, because all fish are paid for at the same price by the cannery men, whether they be caught by traps, by seines, or by gill nets. So the question of price does not enter into it at all.
We fought all this out in the fisheries committee, with the result that it was decided to place the entire matter in the hands of a commission, and Mr. Chief Justice Sloan was given the job of looking into it. Public meetings were held in three of the important towns or cities including New Westminster, to which all interested parties were invited. There, they had the opportunity to air their views fully. The commissioner, following the investigation, then placed his recommendation before the government in 1940, a copy of which I have in my hand. He recommended that the seines be confined to a small area in the gulf only. Now we come to 1942; and under the excuse that more food was required for Great Britain and other countries, seines were allowed into a larger part of the area. This is now the fourth year since 1942, the year of the big run -it takes place every four years-and of course the seines want to get in there again. When the hon. member for Comox-Alberni says that the seine fishermen were asking for something that was fair, I must conclude that he has not read the correspondence which has come to the department, because not only are they asking that the area be allowed to an extent similar to 1942, but they are asking that they get right back to the position in 1933, and take the whole thing right up to the mouth of the Fraser river.
What did they do when they were in the mouth of the Fraser in 1933? They cut the fishermen's nets. Gill net fishermen could not fish in there at all because of the number of seines in the area. Then the matter of quality arises. The commissioner invited cannery men to give evidence in this particular. They did not try to prove nor could they prove that fish caught with one type of gear were better than those caught with another type. As a matter of fact the fish from the two or three types are usually dumped on the wharf at one time, and one can not distinguish whether fish had been caught by gill nets or by seines.
As to the point made about fish with no food inside them being of better quality, I believe there may be some validity in the argument, as it has been put forward by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, in regard to pink salmon. Pink salmon may deteriorate as they go farther up the river. But I can say now without fear of successful contradiction that the sockeye salmon that is caught right up in the Fraser river, and as far up as

the constituency represented by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, produces the finest quality of canned salmon that can be found anywhere. That has not been disproved. As a matter of fact it has been found that the salmon are of better quality when there is no food or feed in them. I am sorry we have not more time to go into this matter at greater length, but owing to the nearness of the end of the session one does not have an opportunity to give as much time to the subject as its importance demands. It is a question, however, of the greatest good to the greatest number.
We are accused of fighting for the individual fisherman. Let me point out that seine boats have been proven to be large, mobile trap nets. Nothing escapes, once the circle goes around the fish. Immature fish and all other kinds are caught within the seine net. We claim that not only does the seine net catch immature fish, but that it interferes with schools of fish by breaking them up, and delays their progress up to the spawning beds. That is our contention. So it is not a matter of our fighting politically, although even if we were fighting politically I cannot see any disgrace in fighting for the people one represents. Surely one need not apologize for that. I approach the matter, however, on broader grounds-because there are fishermen in my riding who operate or work on seine boats; but a greater number of them operate and own their boats and gill nets.
I do not know whether I have answered fully the statement made this afternoon, but I draw the minister's attention to the fact that there should be a better reason for opening area 17 this year than was given in 1942. The minister has the report of the royal commission which investigated the matter fully, and I say the conditions have not changed since that time.
I shall pass on to one or two other matters which I have in mind. Have any steps been taken by the minister's department to popularize the consumption of fish? It is a remarkable fact that during the war the consumption of fish dropped considerably in Canada. I have the authentic figures given by one of the departments in Ottawa.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Do those figures take into account the very fine fish we get from Mink lake and other lakes in North Renfrew?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
One always likes to hear a
member get in a word for his riding. I have no doubt that wonderful fish are caught in that district, but they are caught by sportsmen, and the figures here apply to consumption from commercial sales. I simply want to draw to the attention of the minister what other countries are doing with regard to the sale of fish. For instance, in Newfoundland they are starting an air service to deliver fish so that it will reach the public as fresh as possible. The same thing is being done in Southern Ireland, where they intend to fly fish and fish products right across to England so that the public may obtain these in as fresh a condition as possible. This is bound to create a greater market for their fish. Perhaps the minister when he speaks will tell us what steps are being taken in that direction.
I should like to deal with a matter mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver East, the depletion of our fish. In 1944 the department received a brief presented on behalf of twenty companies and the fishermen's union, which drew attention to the fact that the fish in almost every fishing district in British Columbia were becoming depleted and production was gradually going down. I have said to many returned men, and I say it now to the minister, that it would be unfair to encourage many more men to enter the fishing industry on the Pacific coast. At the present time that industry has about all it can stand profitably. I believe there are now something like 4,000 gill net boats down in the Fraser river waiting for the great Adams river run of salmon which is now heading through the straits to the spawning beds in the upper reaches of the Fraser river. It is not entirely correct to tell ex-service men that there is a great future for them in fishing. Only so much fish is available in each year and the greater the number of the men that enter the industry, the less there will be for those already in it.
I should like to draw the attention of the minister to something which was mentioned yesterday. Our share of the world production of fish is very small indeed. We have done practically nothing to develop fishing away out in the open waters. I notice that the United States has taken steps to encourage new types of fishing and have besides discovered various new kinds of fisheries off the shores of Washington and Oregon, and also off Alaska. They have discovered sardines, herring and other types of fish, and are taking steps to encourage their fishermen to leave the inside fisheries and go out into the open waters. If we are to encourage men to enter the fishing industry, something more will have to be done, and I am suggesting that they be assisted to go out into the open waters on the Pacific ocean and catch varieties of fish available there rather than to keep close inshore and thus cut down the livelihood of those already in the industry.
Exports of fish are down. We did export a considerable amount during the war, but exports have fallen off over a number of years. It may interest the committee to know that in 1879 there were more men employed on the fishing boats on both coasts than there are at the present time. It may be true that they are catching more fish by better and improved methods, but the fact remains that if we are looking at this matter from the employment point of view, our fisheries will have to be developed with a much wider outlook than that which has prevailed during the past fifteen or sixteen years.
When the minister speaks I should like him to deal with this matter and to tell us also what steps are being taken to make fish more readily available to the public. Besides the need for new blood in the department in the way of fisheries experts, we need a more vigorous policy. I have here a calendar put out by the Health League of Canada. The picture here shows milk, meat, bread, eggs, cheese, beef, carrots and potatoes, but not one picture of fish.

What is the Health League

more fish to our people. We shall have to see that the fish is made available in a fresher state. There is more protein value in fish than there is in any product produced on the land, and I shall have a little more to say about that when we reach the item.
Another matter: What is the department doing about the production of fish flour? South Africa is producing fish flour, and it has been found that the addition of this flour in the manufacture of bread makes a more nutritious product. maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I expected that this debate would be finished some considerable time ago, and as I had to attend a committee meeting I sent my questions in written form to the minister in order to save time. However, having listened to hon. members from British Columbia and the Atlantic coast I feel that I must rise to congratulate them upon the wonderful story they have told. It has been a great education for me. I have never visited British Columbia, but I am hopeful of doing so soon. I have heard about salmon, I have heard about lobsters, I have heard about sardines, and it has all been new to me. If the fisheries of Manitoba were not under provincial jurisdiction I would like to tell the committee how wonderful the Winnipeg goldeye, the Winnipeg white. fish and the Winnipeg pickerel are.
I concur in a great deal of what hon. members have said regarding the fishing industry as a whole. The member for Charlotte talked about the price of fish, and that is what the fishermen are really concerned about-the price. I hope that the minister will see that the fish support board does a real job. I do not know whether he has a fisherman on the board; if not, I think he should have, because the fishermen have a real interest in the work of the board. We had an instance of the value of that when we saw various hon. gentlemen getting up in this house and talking about the fishing industry which they really knew something about. We should have men like that on the board, and then I think the fishermen would get better justice done to them than they have ever had before. If the price can be maintained in wartime it can be maintained in peace. The surplus fish should become our necessary reserves in cold-storage plants. It will perhaps be a new way of doing business,

but if it is a good way, the government could provide the cold storage and other facilities required.
I congratulate the minister upon bringing new blood into his department. I think it will work for the benefit of the fishing industry in general. I shall not take any more time. I have given the minister my questions; I know he will answer them as he has done in the past, and that is quite satisfactory to me.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I have listened with
interest to the speeches made by hon. members on the fishing industry. Sometimes hon. members of this house must have felt a bit bored when members from the prairies pursued their agricultural objectives, but I want to assure these gentlemen that we have been profoundly interested in the problems of the fishing industry, and I should like to congratulate them upon the way in which they have presented them. I know that my constituents will feel equally interested with me if I can explain from the Hansard report of my hon. friend's speeches what they have tried to tell us. We would not offer any solution, because obviously there is disagreement among hon. gentlemen who have spoken, and probably honest disagreement. But I can assure them that so far as our people on the prairies are concerned, anything they can do to help the fishermen of British Columbia and the maritimes will be done without question. We appreciate what they have told us.
Will the minister be good enough when making his statement to tell us whether .items 78, 79 and 90 will be applicable to the provinces and to our very small fishing industry in Saskatchewan?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I am not going to make a speech on the fishing industry, because we have no commercial fishing in my riding. It is a paradise for those who want fishing for sport. But in my riding there are firms which supply the fishermen, and therefore I am very much interested in commercial fishing. I understand that during the last year our foreign markets for fish have dwindled. I would like the minister to explain why, if he can give us the reason. Perhaps the minister would also tell us whether his department or the Department of Trade and Commerce is out after new markets for our commercial fish, and why it is that we have lost these markets. Is it on account of price, or on account of quality? Is it because of poor inspection on the part of the department here?

Supply-Fisheries
I should also like to know what quantity of British Columbia salmon is to be exported this year, both frozen and canned, and what quantity will there be for home consumption. During the war years the Canadian housewife has not seen a can of salmon, although we are supposed to have had some 200,000 cases on the domestic market last year.
The member for New Westminster mentioned the drop in the domestic consumption of fish during the past few years. The riding of Peterborough, which I represent, during the last few years has received fish from the Atlantic and the Pacific, but mostly from the Atlantic, and it has been of extremely poor quality. That is the reason why in my opinion the consumption in Canada has dropped. The best quality has been exported and the poor quality kept at home. I have heard not one but a number of housewives say in the fish stores: Why can we not get some decent fish?

speechtext: What kind of fish is the hon. gentleman talking about?

speechtext: Salmon.

Any salmon, frozen or
fresh.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: From Gaspe or British Columbia?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: We seldom get British Columbia salmon.. The hon. member for New Westminster brought out another aspect of the matter, namely, the preparing of fish. I think that the department should put out a really attractive folder, not a halfhearted one, but one that will really show the housewife in how many ways British Columbia salmon, for instance, can be attractively cooked and served.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: You can eat British Columbia salmon raw and it is still good.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I have eaten raw fish caught off the island of Hawaii, sliced thinly by the natives in their little boats and put between two slices of bread. I was nearly starving and I ate it, but I have never tried British Columbia salmon that way. I would emphasize the necessity of getting out, not a book, but an attractive folder showing how to cook different kinds of fish and then distributing it among the fish stores, particularly in central Canada, where it would be made available to the housewives, thus letting them know in how many attractive ways fish can be cooked and served.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I desire to express my appreciation to the members from British Columbia and the maritimes for the able way in which they have presented their opinions. The only one regret I have is that they have not elaborated on their problems because we have reached so late a stage in the session. Next year they should make up their minds to present their case one hundred per cent, no matter how late the estimates may be brought in. They have a case, and a very important one, and it ought to be presented in a thorough and effective manner. So far as I am concerned they have a standing invitation and a welcome to take all the time they want to air their problem so that we can come to an understanding of the various aspects of this important fishing industry in Canada.
In a country as large as ours, with such varied interests, each area is apt to forget the importance of the other areas which constitute the rest of Canada. We cannot hear too much about the facts pertaining to the industries of the country. This country either stands or falls as a unit. I have always rejoiced that there was at least one member in the house from the two central provinces who appreciated the necessity of seeing to it that all Canada was prosperous. I refer to the member for Davenport. How many times has he not stood up in the house and told us that you cannot have a prosperous industrial Canada unless you have a prosperous rural Canada? And I am sure you cannot have a prosperous industrial or rural Canada unless you have a prosperous maritime Canada. We stand or fall as a unit. Our interests are integrated; they form a closely woven pattern.
The questions of price and of markets are troubling fishermen just as they are troubling the producers of wheat'and other agricultural and primary products. I am not minimizing the importance or the difficulty of the problem involved, but somehow in this country we must devise ways and means of guaranteeing a market so that the people who produce will know that they will always have that market, and of guaranteeing a minimum price so that they will know that they will have a price at least above a given floor. I see no way in which this can be done except by dominion government subsidies.
The hon. member for Charlotte was, I believe, on the right track last night when he submitted that there must be a floor under the product. There is, I repeat, only one way in which that can be done, and that is by dominion government subsidies. We must face the necessity of providing such subsidies, just as in the west we expect a subsidy under the price of wheat, and we shall expect one under
Supply-Fisheries

the price of meats and other primary products. It will involve a good many details and technical studies of monetary affairs and all that, which we do not wish to go into at the present time.
There is another matter which is quite important, and that is the question of seeing to it that the man who does the work gets the pay for doing that work. Unquestionably the man. who is entitled to the major portion of the income from fishing is the man who goes into the water and catches the fish. Measures must be taken to see to it that that man gets the major portion of the income from fishing. Such has not been the case up to the present time by any means. The necessity for it was well brought out by the member for Charlotte and other members in their speeches. What public or social mechanism must be established in order to give the guarantee to which I have referred is a matter for grave consideration by the members of this house, and particularly by members who come from the areas affected. If they will devise what they consider to be an effective mechanism, and then come to the house and speak boldly and straightforwardly and tell us what they think has to be done, and how it must be done, they will find that they have earnest listeners at least in my group, and I am sure in the group to my right, who are deeply interested in such matters.
It may be necessary for the fishermen in the maritimes to organize themselves into a pool, probably a great cooperative producing organization, a great cooperative processing organization, a great cooperative marketing organization. It was facing problems such as the maritime fishermen face that caused the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan to build the great pools like the Alberta wheat pool and the Saskatchewan grain growers organization. It may be necessary for the people in the maritimes to organize a pool the object of which would be to purchase the product and process and market it where necessary. They may require a good deal of government assistance to that end, and a good deal of leadership to attain the objects that must be reached. I have often been impressed by the way the British Columbia fruit growers have gone about their problem. The member for Kootenay West has told us several things about what they did. They almost remade the situation for the fruit producer in British Columbia by attacking their problems cooperatively. They grade and market and control the industry cooperatively. The same may be necessary for the fishing industry.

I will say no more at the present time, but I assure members representing the maritime constituencies that when they present the problems of their constituencies they are not speaking to deaf ears or inattentive minds.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I am not going to take up more than a few minutes. I am merely going to tell you why housewives are not buying more fish. It does not matter how good your cook book is, if you smell your fish when you begin to unwrap it you will not like it, and I think this particular phase, the consumption of fish, is going to narrow down to distribution. I am sure that people on the prairies love British Columbia salmon, and when we go to British Columbia we haunt your sea food places. We have feeds of oysters, crab and fresh cod fillets, and I am equally sure that if we went to the maritimes we would do the same thing; we would want to get our fill of the excellent sea foods that abound in those waters. But there are thousands upon thousands of people who live far from the source of these sea foods, and our greatest difficulty has been in. getting sea food that is really attractive. We could depend on canned salmon and canned sardines, because the time lapse between the moment when the fish come out of of the sea and the moment it went into the cans was controlled. But the time lapse between the moment the fish goes into the refrigerator car, or whatever it is they use to ship the fish in, and the journey over the prairies to the local butcher shop, seems to be a sort of indefinite quantity. I think the quick freezing method is something that should be explored, and research should be carried on in the interests of the Canadian family. We can go to almost any store and buy fresh frozen peas, blueberries, strawberries or corn on the cob and take them home and have the very finest flavour, colour and texture preserved in that way. I think that quick freezing applied to sea foods would preserve the freshness as nothing else would, and I would urge the minister to try to do something about the handling of sea foods for people remote from the coast. In our country we confine our fish season to winter because then we get fresh frozen fish. It is the only thing we cam trust. Fish can be like the curate's egg-good in spots. You only need one feed of that sort of egg or that sort of fish, and you do not want to see it again in months. One batch of not-so-fresh fish can ruin your appetite for that commodity. We want your fish. We like it and we have far too little of it. We would

Supply-Fisheries
buy it if we could buy it in such a condition that we could be sure when we served it our families would like it.
I wish to assure hon. members that we are also interested in the incomes of the fishermen. I have been fascinated by the story of fishing. We are deeply indebted to hon. members who have given us so much information on this matter yesterday and to-day. I wish to assure them that we want good homes in the east and in the west; we want good family incomes for fishermen. We do not want poverty-stricken fishing villages any more than we want poverty-stricken prairie villages. But I shall not attempt to tell hon. members how that should be accomplished. From the point of view of the housewife we would buy fish if we could really enjoy the fish that we buy. Until the quality, the method of handling and transportation are improved and treated differently, we shall not promise to buy fish that we can smell.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. F. G. BRIDGES (Minister of Fisheries):
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I had hoped that it would not be necessary for me to make any statement on the first general item of the estimates. Having listened to the general remarks of the various members for a period of about four and a half hours, I have a feeling that it would be difficult for me to reply to all the questions and suggestions which have been made. However, there will be another opportunity when certain individual items come up, and I can make some remarks on those items. In the meantime I seem to have been pressed to make a few remarks on this occasion, and I do not wish to disappoint hon. members by not doing so. At the same time I have a feeling, as I said before in committee, that one does not wish to make a speech with the result of blocking his own estimates. I am perfectly frank about that.
First of all I should like to congratulate most sincerely and most heartily the speakers whom we have heard during consideration of these estimates. I would say without hesitation that two of the hon. members who dealt with international problems and the problem of the continental shelf, the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, one from the west and the other from the east, excelled themselves. The speeches which they delivered on an intricate and ticklish subject were most interesting and instructive. I listened to other speeches with a great deal of interest. They offered criticism of a constructive nature, and this, I assure hon. members, I do appreciate. In a way I am pleased that we should have had so much interest taken this year in the estimates of
the Department of Fisheries, even though they have been presented at such a late date. For many weeks I have been most anxious to get these estimates before the committee, and even at this time, considering other estimates which have to follow, those of the Department of Fisheries have not been placed anywhere near the last position.
May I come back to the questions raised by the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. These are really international questions, and no doubt will be dealt with when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs are before the house. The question of the continental shelf is a most interesting and ticklish one, and one which will require a great deal of study. I cannot do more than assure hon. members that the matter is receiving not only the study of my department but also the study of the Department of External Affairs, which has been consulting my department in this matter. However, if any announcement is to be made or should be made concerning any policy of the kind, it would be, as hon. members know, a matter of high government policy and the announcement would eventually be made by whoever is presiding over the Department of External Affairs. I therefore tell my hon. friends that I cannot say very much about the question of the continental shelf.
I was interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Charlotte. Several constructive suggestions were made by him. As to the work of the fisheries research board and the question of lobster hatcheries, I will deal with that on one of the individual items. With regard to the question of floor prices for fish, I would advise the hon. member that on our statute book we have the Fisheries Prices Support Act, passed in 1944, which sets aside $25 million for that purpose. However, as yet the actual effective section of the act, namely section 9, has not been proclaimed by the government. This is a matter which is receiving the consideration of myself and of the department. I can frankly say that the problem is not an easy one to solve. I have exactly the same feeling as he has, that every effort must be made by this department to give the same protection to those engaged in the fishing industry as is given to those who are engaged in agriculture.
I should like to refer for a moment or two to area 17 on the west coast, concerning which some comments were made by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi. After listening to the remarks made by him and by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, the hon. member for Vancouver North and the hon. member for New Westminster, I am sure hon. members will
Supply-Fisheries

realize what a difficult position I am in at this time. It is not easy to be in a disagreement or in a quarrel with my friends from British Columbia, even when they are all against me, but when you have one on one side of you and another on the other side, and they are against each other and you are in the middle, it is a very unpleasant situation. I should like to point out to them that the matter is receiving careful consideration by the department. Mr. A. J. Whitmore, the director of western fisheries, who knows as much as anybody knows about fisheries in British Columbia is, I believe, on the scene. He went west last week. He is keeping me posted and advised regarding the matter.
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for New Westminster, some years ago a royal commission was appointed and a careful investigation was made by Chief Justice Sloan. He made certain recommendations. Some members of the committee wish me to stand by the recommendations contained in the Sloan report; others wish me to go against or change those recommendations. In assuming an office such as this, a position which I have heldi for only a year, it is not easy for a new minister to make up his mind to go against the recommendation of a royal commission appointed by the government of Canada. But it is my duty and my responsibility as Minister of Fisheries to see that this year Canada gets her fair share of the salmon.
The hon. member for Peterborough West asked a monent or two ago about the quantity of canned salmon which would be available for domestic consumption this year. Some weeks ago I made a statement in the house that some 500,000 cases would be available for domestic consumption. At that time I pointed out that it would be some months before this canned salmon actually got on the shelves in the grocery stores across Canada, because then fishing in British Columbia had just begun, and it is of course still being carried on. I might add that 500,000 cases is approximately the equivalent of what was the average annual consumption of British Columbia salmon in Canada before the war years. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-

speechtext: Before the minister leaves that, will he refer to the question of foreign trade?

speechtext:
I think the hon. member realizes that the question of foreign trade comes within the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce. So far as the government of Canada is concerned the buying and selling of fish to foreign countries would have to be done through the Canadian

Commercial Corporation which has recently been set up. The Department of Fisheries does not actually engage in foreign trade; it merely gives advice to the Department of Trade and Commerce when we are asked for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS

Yes, but the minister's
department would know why we are not holding these foreign markets.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: For a period of three years or more we have had, under international agreement, the combined food board, and under the jurisdiction of that board the salt fish was allocated and later canned fish, to different countries. We got our fair share of the allocation in exactly the same manner as the other countries received their fair share of the allocation. It is purely a matter of rationing to the requirement countries of the world the fish that is available.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: But we have definitely lost the trade.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
No, I would not admit
that.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Well, have not two European countries taken our fish markets away from us?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
No. I would advise my
hon. friend that they have been out of production.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
That is not the way I
heard it.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Well, I am sure my hon. friend will admit that they were out of production as far as competition with us during the war years was concerned.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I understand that at the
present time Great Britain is taking a lot of our foreign market for fish.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
The Department of Fisheries has no information to that effect.
Coming to the remarks made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, I would like to compliment her. I was pleased to find that the only lady member of the house is taking such an interest in the Department of Fisheries. She approaches the matter from an entirely different point of view, that of the housewife, which is probably the most important way of approaching it. She made some reference to quick freezing. I would advise her that this matter has been under constant study for some years by officials of the fisheries research board of Canada; it has been one of their major investigations, and as a matter

Supply-Fisheries
of fact it was through our fisheries research board that the overhead bunker car was developed for the transportation of frozen fish. I do not believe that as yet many of these cars are available to either railway, but more of them will be added this year. They have proved themselves more than satisfactory, and I take considerable pride in stating that the development of the overhead bunker cars is one of the accomplishments of the fisheries research board.
As I said at the outset, I do not wish to speak too long, because I know that questions will be brought up on other items of these estimates. If in these few brief remarks I have not dealt with all the questions which have been referred to by hon. members, I assure them that they may bring them up again on individual items and I shall endeavour to reply to them at that time.

Item agreed to.
77. Fisheries inspection, including fishery, officers and guardians, fisheries patroi and protection services, $1,518,150.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
There are a few questions I should like to ask to emphasize certain specific points not raised in connection with the general item, and also to get the department's attitude toward some of these points. I think the minister can answer them briefly. The minister just now gave the government's point of view regarding the control of the continental shelf, and I fully appreciate that it will take some time to work the problem >
out. My first question is this. Pending some arrangements with the countries concerned, what patrol facilities does the department visualize to protect our fishermen?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: This question of patrolling the international waters is in my opinion essentially a police problem. In dealing with this problem it will be necessary-and I can assure the hon. member we are already doing it-if we find that Canadian fishermen are actually being driven off or are having their gear destroyed, that a scheme be worked out between the Department of Fisheries, the Department of External Affairs, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Royal Canadian Air Force. In other words, that is the attitude and the position we are taking at the present time; we are endeavouring to work out some scheme which will be satisfactory to us so that our fishermen shall receive proper protection.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
In view of the fact that it seems to be common knowledge locally in Nova Scotia and in some of the newspapers across the country what nations are involved
in fishing on these banks, is the minister prepared to state officially what nations are concerned?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: The nations which have had vessels fishing on the Quero and adjacent banks, to our knowledge, are the United States, Canada, Newfoundland, Spain, Portugal and France.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Having that knowledge, I would ask the minister if the governments of any of these foreign countries have been approached by any Canadian department, officially or unofficially?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: This is really a matter for external affairs, but I happen to know that none of the nations I have named have been approached as far as the fishing on Quero banks is concerned. As I have said before in this house, we have as yet received no definite statement from any individual fisherman which clearly identifies either the trawler or the nationality of any European or other foreign trawlers which have been fishing on these banks.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister about the origin of the complaints. Were the first complaints received from the fishermen's union, or from the fishing skippers themselves?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: The first complaints were received from the fishermen's union, and if I remember correctly, the date was May 21.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Have all skippers with whom the government has come in contact experienced interference from foreign trawlers?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: No, definitely not.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Have there been complaints from owners and operators other than skippers?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: There have been no complaints from owners who have not also been skippers. In other words there have been no complaints from owners other than skippers.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
We have referred to
affidavits submitted by these skippers. Would the minister be good enough to read to the committee a typical affidavit submitted by a fishing skipper? I suggest those submitted by Captain Leo Corkum of the schooner Irene Mary.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Captain Leo Corkum supplied the department originally with one affidavit dealing with three different instances. Subsequently we received other affidavits
Supply-Fisheries

from him. I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the committee, but if hon. members wish it I shall place part of these affidavits on record. These affidavits describe incidents on April 15, April 23 and May 25. The one respecting April 15 states, in part:
On April 15, 1946, I was under sail fishing on the S/W peak of the Quero Banks-in position Lat. 44.10 N. and Long. 58.35 W on 45 fathoms of water. It was about 10.00 a.m. and I had my trawls set for the day. It was a clear day and the visibility was good. Each trawl had the usual three buoys, marker, flying "black balls" and each buoy would be approx. 4 mile apart. The sea was fairly smooth and the buoys could be quite readily seen a distance of approx. 4 of a mile away.
There were several trawlers, which in my opinion were of foreign registry, fishing near by me but I am unable to identify any of them.
At about the time mentioned above, while my men were engaged hauling the trawls, some foreign trawler approached me from a S/E direction and dragged through part of my trawls, destroying approx. $100 worth of lines and hooks together with the fish we had on the trawls they destroyed. It all happened so suddenly that I did not have a chance to warn him or contact him by radio, in order to avoid the incident. The trawler I am referring to came in from the S/E cut through about half of my trawls and when it turned out in an easterly direction it would be about half a mile away from me. It then carried on its dragging operation farther east. After having completed hauling the remaining part of my traw'ls, I decided to leave for_ elsewhere. I might add, however, that the fishing in this particular area was very , good at that time, but in view of the fact that the foreign trawlers disregarded the rights of other fishermen on the banks I considered it unwise to run the chance of losing more gear.
I am not in a position to say what nationality this trawler was, neither do any of my crew members because we were not close enough to it to be able to obtain its name or number.
The incident of April 23 is almost similar to the one I have just described. One paragraph in the affidavit reads:
At the time I made my investigation, as described above, I did not know what damage, if any at all, has been caused by this trawler dragging through my trawls, however, when my men had finished hauling the trawls set that day I found I had lost about $75 worth of lines and hooks.
The incident on that date is similar in that neither the name nor the nationality of the trawler was secured. With respect to the incident of May 25, the affidavit is as follows:
On May 25, 1946, I was under sail fishing on the east end of the Quero banks-position, Lat. 44.50N. and 57.45 W.. on 26 fathoms of water. It was an exceptionally fine day and visibility was perfect-the sea was smooth and the fish was plentiful at this particular time. All around me I could see anywheres between ten to fifteen foreign trawlers fishing with dragnets. At the time the incident, which I am about to describe happened, occurred I did not recognize any of these trawlers.

It was about 3.00 p.m. and I had my trawls out for my second set-what we call the afternoon set. I had 33 lines to each small boat with the usual buoys on each line, approx 4 mile apart. On the western end of the trawls I had plaeed an extra large buoy which we refer to as a mark buoy. On a clear day and calm sea a person can see this "mark buoy" a distance of about five miles. My trawler was located at the west end of the trawls and my men were engaged dressing the fish from the first set.
At about the time above mentioned I sighted some foreign trawler approaching my trawls from the south. I immediately started my engine and proceeded east along the south side of my trawls in order to head this trawler off. When I got alongside of it, I called and shouted, as a matter of a warning, to the captain and his men who were on deck, but for some unknown reason they did not seem to pay any attention to my warning and signals. It did not seem to slow down any at all until it reached the buoys on the south side of the trawls. He then hauled his nets up, after having brought the trawler to a stop, but shortly afterward dropped the nets again and steamed west right alongside my men who were then in the small boats engaged hauling the trawls. He then passed through between the "mark buoy" and the west end of my trawls, turned starboard in a N/E direction and again dragged in to my trawls in the N/W corner of my set. While this was going on I steamed up alongside of him again and made every effort to warn him to keep away from my trawls but without result-it is true that as they were foreigners, perhaps they did not understand what I was saying, but as this was a clear day there is no reason why they did not see the buoys and also my men who were then in the small boats engaged hauling the trawls. After it cleared out of my gear it continued in an easterly direction and I did not see it again.
As the trawler departed from the scene, after having caused approx. $200 worth of damage to my gear, I managed to secure its number located on the port-bow. I wrote it down on [DOT] a piece of paper and kept it in my possession for some time, however, I later lost this paper and I am not in a position to recall the figures I wrote down.
After completing hauling the remaining part of my trawls, I decided to leave this location and go elsewhere. I then went to the Grand Banks and on my way there I counted thirty-five foreign trawlers fishing in the vicinity of the eastern part of the Quero Banks.
I have made enquiries among my crew members to see if they are in a position to recall or identify the trawler above mentioned, but neither can they recall its description or number.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: These affidavits are highly significant, in that they indicate that although departmental officials asked these skippers specifically to identify the trawlers by nation of registry, in no instance were they able to do so. This gives a pretty good idea of the difficulty the government is encountering in trying to deal with this problem internationally. Can the minister say how many schooners suffered damage, and the approximate dollar value of that damage to date?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Five schooners suffered damage totalling $1,350, and eight schooners

Supply-Fisheries
whose skippers were interviewed suffered no damage at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I do not see why these particular fishermen should waste so much of the government's time over an amount of S75. From my knowledge of fishermen in my part of the country, in the Georgian bay area, particularly around Collingwood, if any person destroyed their nets to an amount of $75, particularly a Spaniard, they would take hold of him by the scruff of the neck and chase him back to his own country. They would not waste the government's time in writing letters. A man who cannot protect his own interests to the extent of $75 ought to stop wasting our time.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I would say to the hon. member that sail chases steam in some cases.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: There are a few things I should like to mention. It would appear to me that some employees of the Department of Fisheries are underpaid in comparison with what is paid in other departments for similar services. One case I have in mind is the crew of the Fundy Rover, a patrol boat in the bay of Fundy belonging to this department. Four men comprise the crew of this boat and they are obliged to be away from home practically the whole year. The deck hand, with whom I am well acquainted, is a veteran of the last war where he was seriously wounded. For his services during the year he is paid $80 a month. It costs him $20 a month to live on board the boat and, when superannuation deductions of $4 a month are made he has about $55 a month to take home. This man is married with a family; he is an experienced seaman and is a war veteran. I trust the department will consider seriously granting a generous increase to the crews of these patrol boats, particularly when men who have been employed in recent months by the department to do similar work and who have had less experience are receiving more than some employees who have served over a great period of years. I would also be interested in knowing why living allowances are paid in some provinces and are not paid to employees doing exactly the same work in other provinces.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I do not have complete control over the matter of wages, because those things are eventually determined by the treasury board. I assure the hon. member that I will make every effort to see that increases are granted, but I cannot always get what I want. Then there are instances where the labour
board must be consulted. I am informed that living allowances are paid only for services in remote sections of the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Will the minister explain what are the remote sections?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: What does my hon. friend mean by living allowances? Does he mean found on the boat?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Yes. These men are obliged to be away from home the year round.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: If it is found that the hon. member is referring to, I am advised that that is applicable only to remote sections of the Pacific coast.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Another matter to which I should like to direct the attention of the department is the necessity of providing office space for fisheries inspectors. Other civil servants such as customs officials, immigration inspectors, postal officials, harbour masters and so on have in most cases been provided with offices by their respective departments. During the past three or four months I have had some experience in trying to get office space for one fisheries inspector, and I have found that there is very little cooperation between the different government departments in connection with furnishing office space. In many cases public buildings are being maintained in towns where fisheries inspectors reside, but they cannot get office space. This discriminatory and selfish attitude should be condemned and, wherever possible, all civil servants should receive exactly the same consideration. When a fisheries inspector uses his own home for office space a fair rental should be paid by the department. I cannot understand why there is so little cooperation between the different departments.
There is one other thing I should like to mention which I believe comes under this same item. My remarks last December were critical with regard to the wages paid to fisheries guardians. Since then, their rate of pay has been increased from $2.25 a day to $2.70. maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I
would remind the minister of the question I asked about the extraordinary situation which exists on the fishing grounds of British Columbia where, in connection with any violation of the regulations, the fishery officer is policeman, prosecutor and judge. If the fisherman does not plead guilty before the fishery supervisor and wants to be heard by a regular magistrate, his licence is taken away until such time as he can be heard. I suggest that either the Department of Justice send magistrates around to the fishing districts or that these men be admitted to bail if they do not want to plead guilty before the fishery supervisor.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: These powers have been in the Fisheries Act for some years.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: That does not make them good.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I do not allege that. Section 5, subsection 2 of the act reads:
Every fishery officer shall for all the purposes of this act and the regulations made thereunder be a justice of the peace during his term of office as a fishery officer.
Apparently that is the section under which he would act as a judge. Then section 35 reads:
Any fishery officer or justice of the peace may. on view, convict any person committing any of the offences punishable under the provisions of this act, or under any regulations made hereunder, and may remove and detain any fish unlawfully caught and any boat, vessel, fishing apparatus or other materials used in committing any offence or in connection therewith, or which such fishery officer or justice of the peace has reason to believe was so used.
Then section 64 deals with confiscation, and it reads in part:
. . . shall be confiscated to His Majesty and may be seized and confiscated on view, by any fishery officer, or taken and removed by any person for delivery to any fishery officer or justice of the peace.
I am quite ready to admit that those are rather strong sections, certainly contrary to anything we are accustomed to in British countries. However, they have been in the act for some years. The reason would appear to be that in these remote sections there are no magistrates. It might be possible to work out a system whereby the provinces would have magistrates in these remote sections, but I assure my hon. friend that sir.ce he has brought the matter up I will certainly look into it further.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
In
the meantime, could not instructions be given to these fishery inspectors, who act as judges as well as prosecutors, that if a man wants to plead not guilty he should be admitted to bail and allowed to go on fishing until he can appear before a magistrate in the fall? I have in mind one case which occurred in my constituency. A father and son were picked up by an inspector. Although the father and son were living together, it was alleged that they were fishing too close to each other's nets. They did not choose to plead guilty. They were men with a long record, and the reason for that long record was the fact that they had always fished in remote areas and were ready to pay a $50 fine rather than be prevented from fishing for the rest of the season. But this time, being Scotch and stubborn, they decided they were not going to plead guilty. They were remanded and the fishery inspector seized their gear. Two or three weeks later they were taken before a stipendiary magistrate and the case was dismissed on the ground that it was trivial. The men went to get their gear and they found that it had been piled in the sun and had rotted. These men had been out of fishing for three weeks; when they went to get their gear it was rotten, and it took them one year to succeed in a damage action against the crown. That type of administration of justice does not bring respect for the fisheries department. I understand that the judgment against the fisheries department was divided as to costs between the fisheries department and the fishery supervisor who made the seizure. I would ask the minister whether the inspector paid his seizure costs out of his own pocket or whether the government refunded that to him.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
My understanding is that
the case has been appealed and a new trial ordered.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: The crown appealed?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS

These two Scotch fishermen fighting for justice launch a suit against the crown for damages, and now the supervisor launches an appeal against the judgment of the court. That is just going to discourage the fishermen from thinking they will ever get their just desserts. They will figure that it is much easier to plead guilty and pay the $50. That only emphasizes

that the minister should bring British justice into the administration of his department.

I want now to ask a couple of questions and I hope for a favourable answer. Has any provision been made to supply a patrol boat for the Fraser river? The reason I ask is that, so far as the Fraser river in my riding is concerned, the only patrol vessels there in the past have been a couple of rowboats, and in certain cases the fisheries guardians had to pay for the hire of the boats themselves.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I am delighted that the minister has assured me that we are to have a patrol boat, but the other part of his answer, that there is a difficulty on account of the shortage of labour-

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS

Is provision being made to keep the fishery guardians on the payroll throughout the year?
The department requires, and quite properly, that these men must have practical experience, must know the fisheries regulations, and so on. Yet in the past, so far as the Fraser river is concerned, these men have been kept on the payroll for only six months in the year. To expect a qualified man, with a practical know- . ledge of fisheries and a thorough knowledge of the regulations, to carry on this work for only six months of the year and then have to seek other employment is nonsense. I have taken this matter up with the minister's predecessor on several occasions, and I ask the minister now whether consideration is being given to keeping these men on the payroll for twelve months in the year. maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: How about the House of Commons stenographers?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS

It is not reasonable to expect these men, who, I expect, would be married war veterans, to work for only six months out of the year for S100 a month and then look out for other employment, particularly since they are required to have a practical knowledge of the fisheries and a thorough knowledge of the regulations, which they must have to carry them out properly.
