maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I raised some objection last year to this vote, which shows a considerable increase. I would ask the minister to reconsider this vote because, in my opinion, the country is not getting full value for the money expended. I am not against scientists and I do not want my remarks to be interpreted that I am, but I know the experience we have had with scientists on the international salmon fisheries commission. If it had not been for the laymen on the commission; if the scientists had been allowed to spend money and do what they liked, we would not have obtained the results we did. Every year the scientists were asking for more money for various objects. I suggest that the minister consider revamping the whole fisheries research board, and that he include on it representatives of the fishing industry, of the canning industry, members of the provincial government and members of his own department.
I challenge any member of the house to refute what I am about to say. I can produce reports which were made by fishery experts forty years ago, which you will now find contained in the reports that are submitted to-day by the fisheries research board, and I contend that they are not doing the work from a practical point of view of the industry. I am not finding fault with the minister because he has not had time to check up on what they are doing; but from the fisherman's point of view, the practical point of view, I submit that the whole set-up is entirely wrong. In fact, had these estimates come up earlier I might have moved that the vote be reduced. I had declared my intention of doing so when they first came before us in November last, but it is too late in the session now to debate the issue fully. Here, however, we have $3,000,000 spent since the inception of the board just a few short years ago. From 1935 up to the present time this amount of money has been spent. I will not say that some good has not been accomplished, for example, in respect of
the freezing method, and some other matters

as well; but I invite any hon. member to go to Nanaimo station and later read the reports, as I have read them, and see for himself what is being done. I do not believe many hon. members have read all the reports of the fisheries research board, and after a careful study of the situation I would express the view that we are not getting the results we should expect. Let me quote the following article that has appeared in the press:
Fish species, fishing methods and modes of processing are considerably different on the Pacific than on the Atlantic coast. Eastern research board members need first-hand knowledge of -west coast conditions, and western board members tour the Atlantic coast for the same reason.
"We now have the money to carry out this travel policy," a research board official told The Standard. "During the war we had to pull in our belts. Now our personnel is increasing and our work is expanding tremendously."

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Will my hon. friend say what he is quoting from?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I am quoting from the Montreal Standard of June 22, 1946. Travelling may be necessary to some extent, but I suggest that last year there were some joy trips taken. We are increasing the amount this year by $198,000, and I would ask the minister for an explanation. I know he has not had time to keep his eye on the situation; but the actual fact is that he and his officials cannot control the board, and if the present tendency is not stopped they will come back next year and we shall find ourselves voting perhaps a million dollars. And what for? If the minister takes up this challenge I will bring reports from experts to prove the point I mentioned a moment ago. I am against the increase and I am inclined to move that it be reduced. I should like to hear what the minister has to say, what view he takes of the proposal I have made, that certain members of the fishing industry be called upon to constitute a practical board to map out a programme for the research board. As matters stand, we are not getting the results that we should look for.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
The fisheries research board comprises nine scientists from various universities in Canada together with two representatives from the Department of Fisheries and four representatives of industry, two from the Pacific coast and two from the Atlantic coast. The members receive no remuneration for their services, except the chairman, who is given an honorarium of $1,000. Travelling and living expenses are paid when incurred by the members in attending meetings or on business for the board. My hon. friend criticizes the

Supply-Fisheries
board. May I read the names of those who constitute this body. I think hon. members will realize, when I do so, that these are not men who would be inclined to waste the public money of Canada. The chairman is Professor A. T. Cameron, university of Manitoba, one of the best known biochemists in the world. In fact, he is professor of biochemistry of that university. The honorary secretary is the assistant deputy minister of this department. The other members are Professor C. W. Argue, of the university of New Brunswick; Mr. J. H. Deane, of Vancouver, British Columbia, who represents the fishermen's cooperative and who, I am sure, the hon. member will admit is a representative of industry. Then there are Professor J. R. Dymond of the university of Toronto, who is extremely well known throughout the country; Professor W. A. Clemens of the university of British Columbia; Professor
J.	H. L. Johnstone of Halifax, Nova Scotia, a member of the faculty of Dalhousie university; Mr. O. F. MacKenzie of Halifax, Nova Scotia -and I am sure he would not like to be told that he was not a representative of industry- Mr. Burke Melnerney of Halifax, who was secretary-manager of the united maritime fishermen. Another member is Professor Pre-fontaine, professor of biology in the university of Montreal. Another member is Professor G. D. Reed of Queens university. Another member is Mr. J. A. Rodd, director of fish culture, of this department; another member is Professor D. L. Thomson of McGill university. Then there is Professor J. L. Tremblay of Laval university, and the last named member of this body is Mr. R. E. Walker of Vancouver, British Columbia, who is with British Columbia Packers. I do not think the hon. member would suggest that he was not a representative of industry.
These are the men who direct the affairs of the fisheries research board and, when my hon. friend criticizes the board, he is criticizing these gentlemen. They are the men who direct its affairs entirely and they come within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries. Therefore I do not hesitate to say that I am proud of the work they have done, and I am happy that the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, speaking yesterday, made fitting reference to the work of the research board.
I should like to read some letters with reference to the work now being done by the fisheries research board, and first I will quote from one received from the Prince Rupert Fishermen's Cooperative Association. This is dated December 28, 1945:
During the past years our membership consisting of approximately ,1,500 British Columbia fishermen has followed with great interest the research carried out by the fisheries research
board's stations across the dominion. We are all mostly interested in the work carried on closest to where our own part of the industry is affected, although we wish to go on record as being keenly interested in the welfare of the country as a whole, and therefore, no selfish interest is our guide in the recommendations contained in this letter.
The research work that is of the utmost importance to us at this time and which we strongly recommend your department to give its consideration is as follows:
1.	The Skeena river investigation started in
1944.	. ' [DOT]	, . ,
2.	The over-all salmon investigation which was actually started in 1945.
3.	The trawl investigation started in 1944.
4.	The institution of oceangraphic studies of sea life in general.
I will not read the whole of the letter, which is a very long one. It is signed by T. H. Sorensen, secretary of the Prince Rupert Fishermen's Cooperative Association. Let me quote from another letter with regard to the present work of the board. This one is from the Deep Sea Fishermen's Federal Union, Number 80 of British Columbia. It is dated Prince Rupert, December 27, 1945, and contains the following statement:
As the annual meeting of the Fisheries Research Board of Canada will be held in Ottawa on January 1 to 10, we wish to express our appreciation of the work carried out to date by this board regarding investigations of the fisheries, and we feel, it should not only be continued in the future but should be extended to all commercial fisheries on this coast, not only for the purpose of propagation, hut it should also be carried on with the view to making recommendations for control of production of any given fishery whenever it was found too heavily exploited.
Then they make certain statements and ask us to do certain things in the following
respects:
(1)	The necessity of continuing the Skeena river investigation to its conclusion.
(2)	The essentiality of increasing the over-all salmon investigation into a full-scale programme.
(3)	The necessity for a more extensive study of the otter-trawl fishing and the populations of fish which it catches.
(4)	The immediate essentiality to institute oceangraphic studies.
There is another communication from the Fishing Vessel Owners' Association of British Columbia, under date of January 4, 1946, in which similar statements are made. They say:
This association appreciates the great value of the investigations being conducted by the Fisheries Research Board of Canada under the guidance of your department. We would be very pleased if you would bring to the attention of the annual meeting of the board our appreciation of their work and our recommendations for future investigations.
I do not know whether the hon. member is criticizing some particular item or some
Supply-Fisheries

special part of the work of the research board; but I do tell him this, that we are living in an age of research. It was my privilege last evening to listen to Field Marshal Montgomery in an address he gave at a private dinner, and one thing he emphasized was the necessity of research. It is research that has accomplished so many things and is responsible for so many advances in this world. In research, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, scientists cannot discover in a day or in a week, cannot discover overnight, the results which they are seeking. A great many scientists are working on the research board and devoting all their time and knowledge to the work they are doing. We have had instances of men with the degree of Ph.D.-and I am ashamed to say it- working for the board and receiving a remuneration of $2,200 a year. If they are not working for love of the work, then I do not know what it is for. If my hon, friend will mention some individual item that he is criticizing I am quite ready to discuss it with him, but if it is a general allegation that he wishes to make or an item which he desires to cht down and which is in the estimates for the fisheries research board, then I must advise him that I shall resist it.

I should like to bring a new matter to the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance, one which affects only a small number of those who were formerly in the civil service of Canada and who, at the time of the outbreak of war in 1939, were no longer in the civil service but were in receipt of superannuation. Some of these men were taken into the armed services in various capacities, having regard to their special qualifications to perform special duties during the war. I am told they were asked to join the armed services because their country needed them in a time of war, and they were in a position
Supply-Finance

to make a contribution which others not so favourably situated could not make. My information is that these people were assured that superannuation would be paid to them during their service in the armed forces, and that superannuation actually was paid, in addition to their pay of rank, up to May 3, 1940.
My further information is that all these persons regarded the payment of superannuation as well as service pay as one of the terms of contract between themselves and the government. Then, by order in council P.C. 51800 of May 3, 1940, the payment of superannuation to these persons was prohibited-not only to them, but to those in the services who had formerly been in receipt of superannuation. At the same time the order in council did not provide for any voluntary retirement in respect of those affected by it. These men had no choice but to remain in the armed services, despite the fact that the terms of service had been changed arbitrarily.
I could discuss this matter at considerable length, but in view of the fact that we are having long sittings to deal with these estimates I shall not do so. I could build up a certain volume of sentiment and establish a strong factual case in their favour. I speak, however, only to bring the matter to the attention of the minister in order that he may make a thorough investigation of circumstances as they affect these few people. Although there are only a dozen or so affected, the principle involved is important, and those who are affected feel they are being unjustly treated.
Civil servants who were actually in the civil service at the time they entered the armed forces were treated much differently. Their periods of service in the forces counted for superannuation benefits, the government absorbing the five per cent of the civil servant's salary, which would ordinarily have been deducted. But those superannuated civil servants who joined the armed services automatically, through the operation of the order in council, lost their superannuation during their period of service in the armed forces. Those whose implied contracts were broken appear to be in a different position.
I leave these facts for the consideration of the minister, at his earliest convenience, in the hope that he may decide that this group should receive further consideration by the department.

The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, provides for the appointment of a comptroller of the treasury for the purpose of maintaining more complete control over the administration of the consolidated revenue fund. The act assigns the following duties to the comptroller: To remit all public moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund by cheque or other instrument as directed by the treasury board; certification that there is a balance available in the appropriations authorized by parliament for the specific service before any issue of public funds shall be made; certification that there are sufficiently unencumbered balances available out of the amount authorized by parliament for the particular service to pay any commitment before the contract or undertaking involving a charge on the consolidated revenue fund is entered into.

Through the comptroller of the treasury we are careful to see that, to some extent at least, our domestic expenditures are guarded. We are not always sure that they are guarded sufficiently, but in any event they are guarded. In the international field we think a similar situation should exist. This country cannot afford in some instances to keep up with the international Joneses. I am not suggesting that as a nation we have done that. speechtext:
I consider it my duty on behalf of a large number of my constituents to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee certain questionable activities of a loan company in Winnipeg. The company to which I refer is the International Loan Company. Prior to 1921, this company was chartered under a provincial act. Then in 1921 it obtained a charter from this parliament, with an authorized capital of $20,000,000. Then they went out into the western provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta to sell their shares. The price of the shares was $100 each, but for some reason or another they added a premium of $20 to the price of the shares, so that if you bought ten shares, worth $1,000, you had to pay $1,200. The applicant for a share obligated himself to pay at least fifty per cent of the value of the share, and the other fifty per cent was to be paid through the application of dividends. The men who sold these shares went mainly amongst the farmers and, so far as my constituency is concerned, farmers of foreign extraction. In 1931 the subscribed capital of this company had reached $5,620,400. Only part of that was paid, the'remainder remaining callable. We all
know what happened after that. We had the economic depression, then years of crop failure, and of course farmers who had subscribed shares were unable to pay up when the call came. The company allowed the shares to stand until a few years ago and then started to forfeit them, shares on which a considerable amount had been paid. At the end of 1945 the subscribed capital amounted to only $1,785,800 from over $5 million in 1931. In 1945 alone, 23,214 shares were forfeited, having a par value of $2,321,400, and there had been paid on them a total of $159,151.35. I have a list of the shares.
I have taken the matter up with the superintendent of insurance and, while, he is sympathetic in connection with the forfeitures, seeing that a considerable amount of money has been paid on the shares, there is apparently nothing that he can do. The loss of capital in my constituency is considerable. Let me cite two typical cases of farmers who bought shares over twenty years ago. They were told that it was a good investment and that by the time they reached the age of seventy they would have a comfortable income besides any other revenue they might get from the shares. In one case a man paid $1,800 in cash, and dividends at the time of the forfeiture amounted to $338.45. In other words, he had an investment of over $2,100 in the company and it was wiped out a year ago. Another man paid $1,500 and his earned dividends at the time of forfeiture were over $400, so that almost $2,000 of his investment was wiped- out.
Looking over the cancellation of forfeitures in 1945-I have a list of them which I received from the superintendent of insurance-I find that there are scores of similar cases, making up a total of over $150,000 which was paid by poor people whose money has been lost through these forfeitures.
There is in Winnipeg a shareholder named George Batho, who has written an open letter on the subject and whom I had the pleasure of meeting. I told him I would mention his name. He is a retired civil servant, a shareholder in good standing. He has interested himself in the matter and spent his own money and time, and he has done a great deal of work to bring to the attention of other shareholders the deplorable conditions under which the shares were cancelled. I should like to read from this open letter which he wrote to the shareholders last month and in which he sets out some of the conditions I have mentioned:
The day in history wherein one man killed and ate his brother physically is, we hope, pretty well past and gone forever. But, in

Supply-Insurance

regard to fortunes, exactly the same trait of character is being exhibited by International Loan Company. About 25 years ago many hundreds of people responded to the suave persuasions of Doctor Argue, who had a monopoly on share selling, and they bought shares. Then some of the purchasers let their better judgment come to the rescue, and they never paid a "red cent" on the contract. About 570 of such non-payers were dropped in 1945. There was nothing whatsoever wrong with that; they should have been dropped many years earlier. But when they were dropped about 400 other persons, who together had paid to the eompany $102,932.28, as applied on paid capital, and $56,219.07, as applied on premium or $159,151.35 in all, also had their rights in the company forfeited and were left with not one cent's worth of value for all their money. It was confiscation of wealth, pure and simple-dog eat dog- big man eat little man-the wealthier ones gobbling up the less fortunate-financial cannibalism. The company really was not violating the present law of the land in doing this: but in many of the cases it was violating all ethical standards known to mankind. People who buy shares in a loan company and who cannot finish their contract ought to get at least part of the shares they have paid for. The company was solvent; it was not in distress to creditors; much of this forfeiture was just wanton confiscation, many of the forfeitures running into hundreds and even well up into thousands of dollars, where in different cases the contract was decidedly more than half completed. To the end of 1945 shareholders had paid $355.550.31 on share contracts that had been wiped out by forfeiture. This is almost 29 per cent of the present assets of the company.
This confiscation followed right on the heels of oft-repeated assurance to shareholders that their investment was secure.
Whether they are big financiers or little, the shareholders of this company should urge upon their members in the House of Commons that the Dominion Loan Companies Act in this respect should be amended.
The guiding gen;us of this company is Doctor Argue, to whom Mr. Baiho refers in his letter, and lately there has come into the scene his son-in-law Mr. Dick. Doctor Argue holds shares amounting to $40,000 paid up and Mr. Dick holds $18,000 worth, and they can do what they like through proxies. I should like to quote again from Mr. Batho's letter.
To-day, for all practical purposes, this company is tied hand and foot by Messrs. Argue and Dick through the use of proxies. Proxies are commonly used in company business, and their use seems to be quite necessary. But in every other company, or practically every other company, the proxies sought are for one meeting only; and the need for these is to facilitate the doing of business in the event of a small attendance at that meeting. But Doctor Argue and Mr. Dick use continuing proxies, the most vicious proxy yet devised, to continue their stranglehold upon the control of the company. The reports of recent annual meetings tell us that the possession of proxies was announced as follows:

[Mr. Jaenicke.l
Ever since this company began Doctor Argue has assiduously gathered proxies day in and day out. At first these proxies were all for himself; then later they were made to be used by either Argue or Dick. A number of these proxies are about 20 years old; the givers of many of them doubtless have forgotten that they ever gave a proxy; some without doubt never understood the nature of the paper they signed; many of the people giving these proxies have lost touch with the company.
With the use of these proxies, having the company entirely at their disposal, these two gentlemen put through resolutions and other business of the company at their will. They entered into an ingenious contract just a few years ago with this company which gives them exclusive right to sell shares, invest the company's money, rent properties and so on, all on a commission basis and on a fixed fee basis, and as to whether or not the company is making money, these two gentlemen apparently make sure that they make money. This is what Mr. Baiho says with respect to the contract:
With all these proxies in their possession, Messrs. Argue and Dick, a few years ago, had the company issue to them a thirty-year contract as joint managers. The terms of that contract may be good or they may be bad; the point is that these two men, using continuing proxies could hire themselves on any kind of contract that did not violate the terms of the Loan Companies Act or the by-laws of the company. Even before the meeting began they knew that the contract was "in the bag."
The present proxy set-up is utterly bad and intolerable.
I would ask the minister to instruct the superintendent of insurance to look into the matter. With proper pressure being brought to bear on this company by the department, I think it could be persuaded, without a change in the law, to reinstate these shareholders who have paid such large amounts of money and whose money, being almost one-third of the total assets, has helped to make the profits and the dividends which the company has earned. I quite realize that an industrial company which assumes public obligations could not in this way have the continuing shareholders bear the liabilities which the company has, but this company never had any public liabilities. The money that these shareholders paid in, along with the money put in by the other shareholders, produced the dividends which they have earned.
I also think there is something wrong with their financial manipulations. The statement of assets and liabilities and of profits and losses which they publish and send to their shareholders differs from those which will be found on file with the department of insurance. Of course there is an explanation. The superintendent of insurance permits certain deductions to be taken from profits, and the

Supply-Insurance
company treats them in another way. In any event they make out their statement in such a way as to indicate that they are making a lot of money and in fact they are not. During the last twenty years they have only earned dividends of an average of 1-73 per cent on the capital investment.
Another suggestion I would make to the minister is that in a case like this where a company has no public liability, no shares should be forfeited unless it is with the consent of the minister or of the court.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
In any event the committee never got the report of the chartered accountants after they had gone into the plant following receipt of the telegram. That is one point I want to make. I have a letter from the same man. It is not confidential, and he states that a copy has been sent to the leader of each party in the house. I am going to read briefly from the letter. If any credence at all can be placed in it I think it supports the position I took in this house two or three months ago, that there should be public hearings before price increases are granted. We cannot allow representatives of companies to meet with officials of the government, no matter how trusted those officials may be, in private and then say that the information upon which the price increase was granted is confidential and cannot be made public. This man says:
Mr. Donald Gordon, chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, accepted the company's selection of facts-apparently without taking the precaution of indirectly contacting individuals acquainted with the costs which might be properly applied against a given period. I realize that Mr. Gordon is greatly overworked and has difficulty in finding and retaining competent men who neither own a business of their own nor plan to return to their previous employment in a particular industry. Nevertheless, I conceive it to be his duty to provide for brief public hearings before granting price increases or subsidies. It is beyond my comprehension that either the Steel Company of Canada Limited or the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board should be permitted to consider "confidential" any data so vitally affecting the cost of living of the Canadian people. Possibly I should add that public hearings in Hamilton would certainly have revealed that:
1.	The Steel Company of Canada Limited was incurring out of pocket losses on some products and was therefore entitled to substantial price increases on such items.
2.	Had these specific increases been granted, a general increase of $2-rather than $5-per ingot ton would have been quite adequate on all products of which the Steel Company of Canada Limited is the sole or principal producer.
3.	The basic steel producers in Canada prefer to manufacture at a loss rather than allot unpopular sizes among themselves (with govern-
Supply-Wartime Prices Board

ment cooperation if necessary) so that each could make a profit on the cumulative demand for most of his allotted sizes.
From the bluntness of my remarks, you may have received the impression that I am a member of some radical group. Nothing could be farther from the truth, as I usually vote for the Liberal party.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Is that the letter to Mr. Gordon?

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: No, the letter to Mr. Gordon is attached, one of the numerous letters to Mr. Gordon, I believe.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: The letter to Mr. Gordon was shown to me immediately it was received.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I am not going to quote from the letter to Mr. Gordon.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
It was along the same line.
Mr, MacINNIS: It is attached to this one. I submit that it is only a matter of prudence for the administration, before an agency of this government grants price increases that affect the whole economy of this country in the way that these price increases have affected it, first to hold public hearings. I hope the government and the wartime prices and trade board will take note of this and see that such procedure is followed in the future if and when further price increases are asked for.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I take it that letter is from Mr. Weber.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Mr. Weber wrote to the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board a month or two ago along the lines indicated in the letter which my hon. friend has read. I cannot say just when, but Mr. Gordon came to me and showed me the letter immediately it had been received. We came to the conclusion that if the charges in the letter were well founded they were most serious. With my authorization, the chairman of the prices and trade board retained Mr. Walter Gordon of Clarkson, Gordon and Company of Toronto, to investigate the matter. Mr. Gordon went there and he had ample time to do so. I do not know whether his investigation was completed at the time the industrial relations committee was sitting, but it is now and I am advised-I have not seen his report-that his report is that without qualification there is no foundation in the charges made in the letter to which my hon. friend refers.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
We are dealing here with a vote of some $11,000,000. As a matter of interest I was comparing it with the vote for the Department of Fisheries and I find it is a great deal larger. It seems to me that we should have

a general statement from the acting minister with regard to this large enterprise which we are carrying on and on which we are spending $11,000,000. Various detailed questions have been asked and answered, but I suggest that we ought to have a brief general statement, without going into detail, of what has been accomplished, what controls have been abandoned, what controls are still being preserved and what is the objective that is guiding the board at the present time.
As I say, I realize that the minister cannot go into a lot of detail, but it seems to me that, when we are carrying on a business at the expense of $11,000,000, some attempt should be made to give us a picture of that business, to show us what is being attempted, what has been accomplished and what still remains to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: The most recent comprehensive statement was made by the Minister of Finance on July 5 and will be found at page 3180 of Hansard. There is very little that I can add to-day to that statement. In addition, there is the report of the wartime prices and trade board covering the period from January 1 to December 31, 1945, and including important developments up to March 1, 1946. That report contains the general outline of the policy during that period and an indication of the policy for the future. There is nothing I can add to the carefully considered and comprehensive statement made by the minister five or six weeks ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I suggest that there have been certain important changes since that time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: There really have been no changes because the minister's statement followed the change in the exchange rate between Canada and the United States and it followed the cessation of OPA in the United States. The minister indicated in considerable detail at that time the changes which were being made in our price control and economic stabilization policy to meet that situation. I could repeat what he said, but I am sure that is not what my hon. friend has in his mind. There is nothing I can add to what the minister set forth in his statement on July 5. The committee will recall that the question was fully debated on the want of confidence motion regarding agricultural implements. So that between those two debates I think the committee has a pretty comprehensive statement of government policy and intentions with respect to economic stabilization.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
The Acting Minister of Finance said that the special firm of auditors

Supply-Wartime Prices Board
which had investigated the claims made by Mr. Weber of the Steel Company of Canada had made a report. Would the minister table it or furnish to the committee a copy of the facts contained in the report? It is not sufficient to say now that the report found that the contentions made by Mr, Weber were not well founded. I think we should have the report or the information contained in it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I had not expected that this matter would be brough up. I can get the report. It may take me half an hour to get it. Then I would have to consider whether it was appropriate to ta' le it. Offhand I do not see any objection to tabling it. I will send for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Would the minister make a statement regarding the supply of two necessary household commodities, soap and [DOT]alt?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
The shortage of salt is a straight strike proposition, which has resulted in a stoppage of production. I have a statement here on oils and fats, which are related to soap.
It reads:
The world shortage of oils and fats is one of the most difficult supply problems we have to face. For a great many years Canada has been far from self-sufficient particularly in respect of vegetable oils. We are normally very large importers of vegetable oils and considerable importers of certain types of animal fats especially inedible tallow.
The current short position in Canada is due in part to reduced supplies of vegetable oils in foreign countries and in part to a decline in available lard produced in Canada. During the war years the serious reduction in vegetable oils was almost fully offset by increased lard production from Canadian hogs. During the past year we have had to face further declines in supplies of imported oils and at the same time a reduction in domestically produced lard.
The available world supplies of oils and fats are allocated by the international emergency food council. Canada has been allocated its fair share but during recent months there have been serious difficulties in the physical procurement of the allocated supplies. We believe that we are now in the midst of the most difficult period and we are hopeful that we can look forward to a moderate but steady improvement within the next two or three months. The wartime prices and trade board has taken a variety of measures to ease the impact of these shortages. It has allocated lard and shortening to bakers and other industrial users on the basis of 80 per cent of 1941 usage; it has encouraged the maximum diversion of suitable fats and oils to edible uses; through its compulsory de-fatting of carcasses order it has saved many millions of pounds of animal fats at the source, a high proportion of which would probably have gone to waste had it remained on the carcass through
to the retail butcher and the final consumer; it has placed temporary limitations on the quantity of fats used in the production of soap.
The current shortage of soap is also due in part to shortages of caustic soda, the supply of which has been seriously diminished by reason of industrial disputes.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Is any collection of fats being carried on as was done some time ago, or has that been discontinued?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
That was done under
national war services. That has lapsed, but the de-fatting order to which I referred has largely taken up the slack.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: What about the household fats that accumulate in kitchens; is that not being used? It is not being collected now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: It can be re-used by the housewife, of course, but no attempt has been made to collect that source of fat.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I think the committee
are not very well satisfied with the minister's statement regarding milk. A little earlier he made reference to OPA in the United States. While I agree that, on the whole, the performance of our wartime prices and trade board is better than that of OPA I noticed in the Ottawa Journal of August 28, yesterday, a dispatch from New York saying that:
Paul A. Porter, office of price administration administrator, said to-day ue would insist on restoring ceiling prices in the United States for fluid milk and dairy products. He said he would ask for the ceiling price of June 30, with subsidies for fluid milk.
I submit that if in the United States they are taking that step with respect to fluid milk, the Canadian government might very well
reconsider its decision to discontinue the producer subsidy on fluid milk.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: There is nothing in that. Their price of milk in the United States is seventeen to nineteen cents. The pricing of milk in Canada was turned back on June 1 to the provincial milk boards, which are free to impose any ceiling they see fit.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: It is not being turned over to the state authorities in the United States. The federal government there is taking the responsibility of seeing that the consumer will not pay more.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: In Canada we have the provincial milk boards. I do not think they have that in the United States. Our provincial milk boards are the best machinery to control the price of milk.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
That was not the policy during the war. It was considered the responsibility of the federal government so that the cost of living might be kept down.
Supply-Wartime Prices Board

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: With the abandonment of the consumer subsidy and the proposed abandonment of the producer subsidy, the control of the price of milk has been returned to the provincial milk boards.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Would the minister say something further about the shortage of salt, which is getting worse and seriously affecting our cheese and creamery production. If something is not done to get a supply of salt, many of our cheese factories and creameries will be up against it to continue production. Would it not be possible to have salt imported from the United States to tide us over this shortage period?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I am advised that salt is pretty scarce in the United States. The shortage in Canada is entirely due to the industrial dispute in the C.I.L. plant at Windsor. If that can be settled the supply of salt will be increased.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: It is reported to me that many cheese factories are having to grind up rock salt to put in cheese, which is not good for the quality of our cheese. Something should be done to relieve the shortage, which is most serious.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I hate to bother the minister but he is tangled up with the most important agency in Canada, so that we have no alternative. I should like to know if any action has been taken by the wartime prices and trade board to remedy a serious defect which has become apparent in its machinery since its establishment. There should be greater cooperation or liaison between the wartime prices and trade board and the national war labour board, which fixes wages. There was a good deal of criticism in the industrial relations committee because of lack of coordination. While Mr. Gordon clearly stated that it was not the job of the wartime prices and trade board to fix wages, and there was no actual representative from the war labour board on his board, except the deputy Minister of labour, who sits in as an observer-

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: He is a member of the board.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Well, in reality the wartime prices and trade board do fix wages. They set prices and ceilings beyond which wages cannot go, and in that way they definitely rule in the field of wages as in prices. Theoretically they may not, but practically they do. Perhaps many of the difficulties in the field of industrial unrest might have been avoided if there were some understanding and if an official representative of the wartime

prices, and trade board and the war labour board sat in and did one job. The committee, when they presented their report to the house, definitely recommended that there should be closer cooperation and some official contact. Has anything been done to implement that recommendation? I think the time has come when we should be perfecting that machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I can only answer by saying I am convinced that there is the closest liaison and cooperation between the two departments of government. There is a certain inconsistency in the hon. gentleman's remarks, because it seems to me, though I may be wrong, that onfy a month or so ago he was saying that it was not necessary to raise prices if wages were raised; that a wage rise did not necessarily mean an increase in prices.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I will not allow the minister to get away with that, because there was never any such statement on my part. What I did say was that an increase in wages did not necessarily mean an increase in prices or an increase in factory cost, because I actually put figures on the record from the Hamilton Steel Company to show why wages had gone up over 40 per cent, but the cost had come down proportionately as a result of increased productivity. That was true in that particular industry. I realize that it cannot happen in all, but the blanket statement attributed to me by the minister is not in accordance with the facts.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I did not suggest anything that could be taken as a blanket statement, but my hon. friend indicated pretty generally that a wage increase did not necessarily mean a price increase.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Before the item carries, I want to put something on the record. On August 28, 1939 I wired from Riviere du Loup to the Prime Minister as follows:
War profiteers taking advantage of war scare ' to exploit people by raising price of necessary commodities of life sugar 45 cents flour 40 cents per bag in a few days stop It is a shame stop Please take means to stop it very urgent. Jean Francois Pouliot.
Release to
Canadian Press, Mr. Flaherty-Ottawa.
Two days later, on August 30, I received the following wire from the Prime Minister:
Jean Francois Pouliot Riviere du Loup, Q.
Situation described in your telegram of yesterday will be given immediate attention of the government.
W. L. Mackenzie King.
I put these on the record because, while I have been responsible to a certain extent for

Supply-Wartime Prices Board
the creation of the wartime prices and trade board, I would not take the whole responsibility for it and for what it has done since its establishment, and I hope that the members of the board will do something other than try to justify their action when they refuse a reasonable request made by any member of parliament. We have an advantage over the members of the board in the fact that we live among the people and are in contact with them, and therefore we ask for a redress of their wrongs. I have a word to say in praise of Mr. Gordon for having closed the office in Cabano in my district. I prefer to have none than to have such trouble with a man who was making difficulty for all the good people who live there. I do not have so much to complain about the board in these later times, but I hope that when representations are made by any member of parliament we shall not speak to deaf ears.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: One question. Is it reasonable to presume that the minister is in favour of the continuation of the subsidy for milk in order to keep the cost of living down?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: That is a matter which will be considered by the government, as I indicated earlier in the evening, and perhaps it would be improper for me as one member of the government to indicate my own views until the decision of the government as a whole is announced.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I think the minister is going to do his best.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I would not draw too hasty a conclusion.

Item agreed to.
489. Commodity prices stabilization corporation, $90,000,000.
Mr.' MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario): Will the minister say a word about this? Unless there is a statement covering the situation, this seems tremendously important. It does not seem to cover the whole subsidy situation. I would suggest that we ought to have the subsidy picture, and I will ask the minister to deal with the question in a comprehensive way.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I will ask the parliamentary assistant to give the detailed estimates.
To answer the latter part of the question, this does cover all subsidies with the exception of producer subsidies which may be paid in the Department of Agriculture and which have been covered, if any, in the estimates of thit department. For instance, there is the producer milk subsidy, the one we have been
discussing this evening. It is paid by the Department of Agriculture and provided for in the agriculture estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: But may I not ask the Department of Finance, which is the father and mother of all these things, to give us a complete picture of all our subsidies so that we may know what we are doing. This is an important part of our life. The impression sometimes gets abroad, I think, that in some mysterious way subsidies do not come out of our pockets, and therefore, it would be well to get the complete picture if we can.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Does that total $90 million?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Import subsidies

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Do the items that the parliamentary assistant has read total $90,000,000?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I left out Wartime Food Corporation Limited, $100,000; administration expenses, $1,200,000; making a total of $90,000,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Where do oranges and other citrus fruits come in, in this total?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: They are not subsidized; other citrus fruits are not subsidized.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
In connection with the firms that have been paid subsidies, would the parliamentary assistant indicate whether they came within the excess profits tax category at the same time? In other words, is the financial position of a corporation considered before a subsidy is granted? If a corporation was in the excess profits tax category, was a subsidy paid?
Supply-Wartime Prices Board

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: We have profit control of most industries, but not on the import subsidies.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: It would appear to me that, before a company became eligible to draw from the public exchequer, it should be necessary that information be submitted that the firm really required these payments before any subsidies were granted. The statement of the parliamentary assistant does not seem to me to be satisfactory.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I have a question along the same line. How are these subsidies arrived at? Take the instance of coffee. It would seem to me that coffee would not be classed as a necessity; it could almost be looked upon as a luxury.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: We take a bulk trading loss on coffee. I do not know what the view of the committee is, but I do not think one can look on coffee as a luxury. I suppose 999 people out of 1,000 in the country have coffee or tea for breakfast every morning. It is just as much a part of their diet as bread is. These items are considered as being items in the ordinary average man's diet, and are not luxury items. [DOT] So far as I know, there are no subsidies on items which can be classified as luxury items.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: When a firm makes an application for a subsidy it would appear to me to be reasonable that the company should submit evidence that it could not operate and make a profit without it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: It does that in order to get an import subsidy. The subsidy is granted in order to obtain supply, not to help the individual importer, but to enable the product to be sold under the domestic ceiling. That is the purpose of the import subsidy. When an importer applies for a subsidy he must show that, without the subsidy, he cannot sell under the ceiling.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Subsidies were paid not only on goods imported but on domestic goods.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
Oh, but in these cases, as the parliamentary assistant indicated, in most industries there is profit control. In the case of the flour subsidy, for instance, there is profit control, and in others. These are the domestic subsidies, but there is a system of profit control. If the person in receipt of the subsidy is in the 100 per cent bracket, to use a common phrase, then he does not receive the full subsidy. There is a profit control imposed, so that he will not receive the subsidy and at the

same time retain the twenty per cent refundable portion of his tax. That has been rigorously enforced.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: Will the minister indicate whether that has been followed throughout all the operations of the wartime prices and trade board? If a firm was in the category of an excess profits tax firm no subsidy would be paid on the operation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I do not know that I can say it is followed in all cases. I am advised that it is followed in the majority of cases.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: .This is a matter of government policy, and it should be quite clear. If a firm was in the position where it was doing a better business than it had done in the basic period it would not seem to me to be in a position where it would require any subsidy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: As I say, it is done in the majority of cases, but in some cases a firm was just not interested. It would say, we will not do business in this commodity; we have lots of others in which we can do business; let somebody else do the business. If it is an important factor in the distributing system we have to take action. In the vast majority of cases, in the cases which really count, that has been the policy which has been followed. In a good many cases the firms have not been too keen on it. They feel it is not fair. Nevertheless we have succeeded in establishing on the domestic subsidies a pretty comprehensive system of profit control and it has worked very well.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: With regard to this $2,700,000 for the wood fuel industry, has the parliamentary assistant a breakdown province by province? How much wood wras purchased under that subsidy arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I am sorry to say we hate not a breakdown of that item. The subsidy is paid by the commodity prices stabilization board, an agency of the board. This is where the vote is, but it is actually administered by the Department of Reconstruction, and in past years, as my hon. friend probably knows, it was administered by the Department of Munitions and Supply because the fuel controller is in that department.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: It is not paid to the producer? That is what I am thinking of.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: It is paid to the agency that sells it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext:
I believe that is correct.
' Mr. GILLIS: Can the minister obtain the figures province by province and place them on Hansard?

Supply-Wartime Prices Board

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS
speechtext: I think the Department of Reconstruction and Supply can supply them. I shall ask my colleague, the Minister of Reconstruction, to get the figures. I would hope that it might take a little longer than we are likely to be sitting here this session, but in any event we shall do the best we can.

maintopic: SUPPLY OF FUEL OIL AND OIL BURNERS

(The statement is as follows:)
Rental Regulations-Eviction Control.
The rental regulations have given some degree of security to tenants ever since rent control was first introduced. Until the summer of 1945 the landlord who wanted to occupy his own house could do so provided that he gave the tenant adequate notice. The regulations were changed from time to time, the length of notice varying from six to twelve months. Without this protection many landlords might have 1 aken advantage of the
Supply-Wartime Prices Board

shortage of housing to demand higher-than-ceiling rents on pain of immediate eviction. At the same time this protection prevented or minimized the inconvenience and suffering that would have been caused by virtue of the housing shortage.
During 1945 the shortage of housing became progressively more serious. Dwellings which were occupied by tenants were being sold in large numbers for early occupancy by the purchasers. At that time the purchaser could obtain possession of the house if it was needed for himself or for some member of his family 3n giving six months' notice to vacate. Tenants who had been served notice to vacate felt themselves compelled, in many cases, to purchase houses and, in turn, to serve notice to vacate on the tenants of these houses. By the early summer of 1945 the prospect of widespread evictions throughout the urban areas of Canada had created a serious social problem. In the city of Toronto alone, for example, there were some 3,500 notices to vacate maturing in the three summer months. Many of these notices to vacate had been served upon families or dependents of veterans. There was no alternative accommodation for the many thousands of people involved across Canada. Consequently, the Government - instructed the Prices Board to enlarge the existing system of tenant protection. This was done by Order 537, which imposed an indefinite "freeze" upon all tenants. At the same time, all outstanding notices to vacate were suspended.
In order to be fair, those purchasers or landlords who had given the tenants the proper notice to vacate were permitted to go before a court of rental appeals for a hearing. The decisions of the appeal judges in thes cases were based upon an assessment of the relative burden of hardship involved as between landlord and tenant. The one other exception to this indefinite "freeze" related to discharged service personnel.
The government recognizes that, in freezing virtually all leases relating to self-contained accommodation, it has drastically interfered with the normal rights of the property owner. This action is justified as an emergency measure designed to avoid far greater dislocation and social distress. Notwithstanding the many individual cases that can be shown to exist where the regulation works great hardship on a man who had purchased a home for the occupation of himself and his family, the situation would be far more desperate if the regulation did not exist. If this regulation were not in force to-day, it would be found that the turnover in houses would be enormously greater, tens of thousands of families would be under threat of eviction, and virtually every tenant family would feel itself insecure. At the same time, the enforcement of rental ceilings would be impossible, in many cases, if landlords were free to give notice to vacate to their tenants, or to threaten to give such notice. It is the extreme housing shortage which has created this situation, and nothing short of a considerable increase in the supply of housing will make it possible to relax this extra-contractual system of tenant protection.
The government is aware that some people have bought houses since order 537 was issued in ignorance of the fact that they could not obtain possession for occupancy. There have been cases where the sellers or the agents concerned have refrained from advising the pur-
[The Chairman.]
chaser of this condition. The government has done everything it can to acquaint the people with the existence of this regulation and cannot be expected to rectify situations of this kind in favour of the purchaser without nullifying completely the purpose of the regulation. It should be noted that, while order 537 sometimes operates	to	make it	impossible	for a
veteran to move into a house which he has purchased in recent years, a much greater number of veterans and veterans' families are protected, as tenants, by the regulation in question.
Special provisions relating to veterans.
The "freeze''	in	question	(order 537) doesnot apply in certain cases where veterans are involved. Under order 511, passed May 14, 1945, where a	veteran (or	his wife)	owneda dwelling at	the	date of	enlistment,	he is
entitled to obtain possession of the property for his own occupation on giving the tenant a specified notice, which is never less than three months. The other exception in favour of veterans relates to the case where the accommodation wras occupied by a veteran at the date of enlistment and where the veteran is closely related to the landlord. In such a case the landlord may give the tenant a specified notice to vacate in order to rent the property to the veteran in question. These exceptions to the "freeze" are fair and equitable. They have the effect of enabling many veterans to re-occupy premises which they owned and which they had rented to others while serving writh the armed forces, or wdiich they had rented from relatives previous to joining up.
In the case of multiple-family buildings order 511 also allows a landlord to dispossess a tenant (after at least three months' notice) in order to rent the accommodation to a veteran who is a close relative of the landlord in question. This further exception to the general "freeze" wras also made in the interests of veterans and was supported by representations from veterans' organizations.
The evictions of tenants which are taking place to-day relate mainly to cases of this sort, or to cases originally decided under order 537 where the balance of hardship wras decided by a judge in favour of the landlord, and where the notice to the tenant has now matured.
It must be admitted that in certain cases it sometimes happens that both parties are veterans, and one veteran may be evicted in favour of another. This only goes to demonstrate the difficulty of extending still further the list of exemptions to the "freeze" on tenants.
Conclusion
The protection nowr given to tenants wras introduced in 1945 because of the emergency caused by the shortage of housing. In that situation it was necessary to take drastic steps to call a halt to the movement of tenants in the interest of the greatest good of the greatest number of people. To be effective, it was necessary to keep the number of exemptions to the rule to a minimum, and the exemptions have been mainly in favour of veterans. The protection of tenants undoubtedly inflicts hardship on a small minority of landlords, and the exemptions in favour of veterans also work hardship on a small number of tenants. In recognizing this we should

Supply-Trade and Commerce
not forget that the regulations are intended to serve the interests of the majority of people, and by and large that objective has been achieved.
Progress reported.
