speechtext:
Finally, we refrained from formal protest, despite our rights under empire trade agreements, against the banning of Canadian manufactured imports from Great Britain, and at a time when we realized that the British people were short of Canadian dollars and had to conserve all their slender supply for the purchase of foodstuffs.
In other words, under the British empire agreements there are certain standards on which we could have stood solid, and said, "You are not living up to your agreement." We did not do so. I realize, of course, that hon. members look upon this party as the party of protection in Canada. I am quite proud to say that, to a limited degree, that is so. We did not protest against this because we realized that here was an international situation, here was an empire situation that meant much to the British people who had sacrificed so heavily when the war was on. We were prepared to do our part to help them obtain so-called American dollars which, in fact, were our dollars.
After referring to all-out cooperation with the British people in their present critical economic struggle, the Quebec Chronicle Telegraph goes on to call attention to a specific British treatment of a Canadian interest which, in the light of all pertinent considerations, seems completely ungracious and to call definitely for correction. The editorial says:
For over half a century Canadian Club or rye whiskey had been imported into the United Kingdom prior to the late war, during which time such a wide popularity was developed for the brand at great expense and effort that it became literally a household word. The last permit for the importation of Canadian Club into the United Kingdom was granted, however, in January, 1941, and since that time repeated applications for further permits have been made without avail. As a result, the good will obtained through the years is being rapidly lost, and will have to be reestablished again, if it can be done, by means of fresh effort and expense.
The editorial then goes on to say that the British attitude is made completely inexplicable by the fact that during the period in which Canadian Club has been persistently embargoed, the United Kingdom has imported spirits from no less than fifteen other foreign and empire countries. In this connection the editorial comments-and I confess I cannot [DOT] bring myself to disagree from the observation -that these imports came from countries whose governments-
. . . take a lively interest in the present and future prospects of their products, while both the Ottawa Department of Trade and Commerce and Canada House remain continuously asleep at the switch.
I say that, not unkindly.

This discrimination against a Canadian product by the United Kingdom authorities seemed so inexplicable to me that I could hardly believe the facts were being correctly stated. I took the trouble, therefore, to look up the most recent official figures of imports of spirits by Britain. Realizing that they had this embargo against them, to my amazement I found that the situation was precisely as the editorial had represented it. During the first four months of this year, spirit imports into the United Kingdom totaled 778,699 proof gallons as against 313,486 proof gallons in the corresponding pre-war period. On their very face, these figures established that, at a time when spirit imports are being barred from Canada by the United Kingdom authorities, they are being admitted at more than twice their pre-war volume from other countries.
I wonder if the minister, in whose qualities of tact and diplomacy we all have the highest confidence-and I say that in all sincerity, because I have had a lot to do with the Department of Trade and Commerce in the prewar period when we were trying to sell to France and other countries, and on those occasions I found no one more cooperative than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I make that statement in all sincerity. I believe he has done everything he could, but I point out that here is something which, while on the surface it might appear unimportant, is in fact of considerable importance. It is important because everything we can sell in a foreign country is important to Canada.
So I say that I believe the minister could do a job in this instance. I believe that, in the interests of the continuance of the close relationship into which we have entered with the British people at the present time, no element of injustice should be left in the picture to breed possible future dissensions. I believe firmly in all the measures we have taken this session to assist the British people economically. But I do not believe that we should acquiesce in discrimination against our trade and see imports, with which we should certainly be allowed to compete, brought in from other countries. It may be that this matter of importing these spirits may not be thought to be important, but I want to remind the minister that, it does not matter what is exported, it is important for the people of Canada. I do not care what we import; it is important for the people of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, you represent a highly industrialized riding as I do. You have in your riding farmers and a rural population. We have to be careful that what we do to-day will be a precedent for the future. We have to do

Supply-Trade mid Commerce
these things in a way that will look after our working men. We have a fight on for higher wages which are supposed to represent better living conditions. I am all for it, but if those higher wages and that type of living conditions are going to jeopardize our position economically with the rest of the world, with low wage countries, with Russia which to-day economically and industrially is the biggest threat we have to face, then I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that we must be careful. He should make a strong protest to the government of Great Britain and make them realize that they cannot do these things against Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I had hoped that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would have opened this discussion with a general statement of the work of his department. I-and no doubt other hon. members-am somewhat perturbed at our lack of knowledge as to just what is going on in the department. Even though we are getting toward the close of the session, we still insist that we have some information in that regard. As far as I am concerned, when the next session rolls around, unless the minister can make arrangements with those who set the orders of the day so that we can have his estimates somewhat sooner, I am going to be prepared to stay a lot longer even though I have to bring a cot into the corridors in order to be able to stick it out.
As I say, we are all concerned about what is going on. Whom are we trading with? What are we trading for? How many trade envoys and other personnel have we? What are they doing?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Good work.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Some one says, "good
work", but that is what we want to have the minister tell us. As I said a moment ago, I was disappointed that we had not a statement from the minister.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: He has not had a chance.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
We hope they are doing good work, but we should like to know more about the work they are doing. We should like to know whether they are all doing good work or only some of them. We should like to know whether some are just making good fellows of themselves at somebody else's expense. We want to know what they are doing in the different countries,
When the meat board estimate was up for discussion I said something which I think I should repeat. Those people who represent us in different countries should make an effort
to sell our articles to the people of those countries. If I am not mistaken, some countries have adopted a policy by which they attempt to follow their products, bacon for instance, right through to the distributor, so that the people buying that product will be certain that they are getting what they think they are getting under a proper trade name. There are many things like that we should have liked to discuss with the minister.
We should like to know whether we are just trading for the sake of trading, or whether we are trading to improve the living standards of the people of this country, in the first place, and to help people in other parts of the world who need help, in the second place. In trading, I realize it is necessary to operate with the idea of having a fair exchange of goods between countries. I realize that with some countries having had to face war for six years or longer economic conditions have been upset. I realize it is difficult to get off to a proper start. But I would point out that when we are trading we should always bear in mind that the people of our country-I have pointed this out in the house time after time-are entitled to a decent standard of living from the things they are able to produce from our natural resources.
We do not want to curtail in any way the movement of necessary supplies that can be sent to the countries that need them. Very often officials in the department become so much concerned with the carrying on of trade that they remind me of some of the old horse traders we used to have in the days when horses had still some attraction to many people. Many of those men traded horses just for the sake of trading, even though at times they might not make anything out of it. I am afraid we still have some old fashioned horse traders in the Department of Trade and Commerce.
As I told the minister last session, the department should become a little more up to date. In this connection I should like to quote from a letter which I received from a person who lives forty or fifty miles from my own home and which arrived only this morning. The things which he says in this letter are causing me considerable concern, because I know they apply not only to that neighbourhood but fairly generally over the prairie provinces. He said:
Crops that looked like 40 bushels to the acre were caught by first-six weeks drought that burned them up bad. A heavy frost came on July 22. Then we had a hail storm that further reduced the yield an d thr n to top it off, when

Supply-Trade and Commerce
we started to cut, all the low spots in the grain were under water. (Result, about 15 bushels to the acre of grade No. 3 or 4.
So many people were going about the country talking about a bumper wheat crop as if it were in the bag already, when the wheat was only coming into the head. This writer continues:
Of course we cannot buck the elements, and years of adversity, as well as a few good crops have taught us to take things as they come. But when man-made laws interfere with garnering the little crop we have got, it is time to complain.
May I interject here that when I have an opportunity to speak with this man I shall try to explain to him that it is not only manmade laws he has to contend with, because very often officials in certain departments who like to show their authority put a few additional regulations into effect. I just point that out, because often some people would lead us to believe that it is the law which is interfering with the free movement of people and trade, when often it is not the law but regulations. When we are talking about trade we should never forget that our best customers are the people right here in Canada. We must remember the importance of trading with our people in the various provinces of this country. When this man complains of man-made laws I want to emphasize that very often the real fault is man-made regulations which have not the status of law, although some people would like to put that over. He goes on to say:
I have a plough on order, paid for over a year ago, but cannot get it. There are thousands of acres waiting to be swathed and combined, but machinery is not available. So we fetched out the old binder but repairs are hard to get. You have really no idea of the thousands of dollars that are spent every day on telephone calls to locate some piece of machinery or repair, and the thousands spent on travelling from town to town to locate some sorely needed piece of repair-not counting the loss of time.
That is the condition which also prevailed last year. I remember I was in a little town about twenty-five miles from my home one day and I met a man wrho lived another twenty-five miles from there. We went into a little cafe and had a bite to eat, and he told me that he had spent all that day chasing up and dowm the country from one point to another trying to locate a few repairs he needed for his machine so that he could go ahead with his harvesting. This writer continues:
Two of my neighbours travelled all the way to Wisconsin, the only place where they could get repairs for their tractor and other machinery.
[Mr. Burton.1
That is a fine how-do-you-do. We go to work and export farm machinery and parts to the United States, and then some of our own Canadians have to cross the line to get repairs they need for their own machines to take the crop off in this country, crops that not only we in this country need but other people whom we are proposing to help by sending them food and machines and other things.
As 1 said before, I want to cooperate as much as possible with the minister, but there are some questions which we want answered, and I can assure the minister that he will have the appreciation not only of myself but also of my colleagues if he will so arrange matters with the powers that be who make the orders of the day for this house that his estimates come up for consideration earlier in the session.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Just a few words, Mr. Chairman. But first let me say to the hon. member for Humboldt that if he wants that procedure to be followed in the house he should not say that he will tell us more than he has done to-day because, if he does that, the estimates may come only after the session is over. speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that I have not taken up one fraction of the time he has in delaying the consideration of these estimates.

speechtext: My hon. friend must not consider what I said as a reproach. It was a most amicable suggestion because I want the same thing too, and I will tell the minister that if he will bring his estimates up earlier in the session I will make only five-minute speeches in the house.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I will tell you that trade and commerce is the most important department in this country now that the war is over. Trade is the very lifeblood of our country, and those who do not believe that have not the least notion of the needs of this country in the postwar period. We have no information at all about trade. Trade does not exist. A trade of gifts, a Santa Claus trade, is not trade at all. Santa Claus is not a big merchant; he is not a big business man. But Canada is Santa Claus.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Santa Claus makes a lot of money.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
No; other people make a lot of money through Santa Claus. Santa

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Claua is not a businessman, according to one of the greatest men whom my hon. friend admires and supports so much, Doctor Chisholm. According to Doctor Chisholm, Santa Claus does not exist.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I am here to do my duty and I will perform it. This is not a joke at all. Trade is the most important thing in this country in the post-war period. It is important to fhe businessman, to the farmer, to the country storekeeper, to all those who are engaged in trade. All the men employed in industry benefit from trade, and if they ever knew that in this House of Commons a member who defends them is interrupted by some hecklers who are anxious to go home, and who unfortunately do not go, they would be astounded. How can a man go before the electors of his constituency and ask for their votes when he is untrue to his duty as a member of parliament and when he does not realize the importance of trade in the post-war period? I am most indignant on behalf of my constituents at these interjections, and I should like the constituents of those members who shouted out a moment ago to be here in this House of- Commons and see the sad performance of their representatives in these late hours of the session.
If the estimates come before us late in the session, it is not our fault. These are some of the most important estimates that come before us because, if the Department of National Revenue succeeds in collecting taxation, it is precisely because of the benefits that will have come through trade to our merchants and to all our people in this country. Therefore trade is a vital thing, and it is just as vital for the farmers as it is for the industrialists and the working men.
What is the first condition of trade? The first condition of trade is economic independence. 1 repeat now what I said during the war, and which was not denied by a Tory to the core like the former leader of the opposition, the former member for York-Sunbury, Mr. Hanson: We must be economically independent. That is just as true as sunlight at noon. We must be economically independent, meaning by that that our commercial agents and representatives abroad shall not be under the tutelage of any other country and shall not have to report to British consulates, agents and British ambassadors.
The minister will remember that when the only consul general that we have, Mr. Scully, was appointed to New York, the Prime Minister announced that he would work in close cooperation with the British authorities. That
is on record in Hansard. It is a fact, and if the position of our agent were such that there should happen to be a difference between English and Canadian businessmen, the Canadians should have the full support of our government. But in order to have it they should be prefectly independent and should not say to those of other countries, "Go ahead and we will follow you." I do not say that for the purpose of deprecating the merits of the minister, because I have profound admiration for him and, besides that, he is a personal friend of mine. But in these matters we must try to be realists and must realize the importance of both export and import trade. I have the more sympathy for the minister in that he is not the master of his department. There is the stabilization board, which is under the Minister of Finance, and he has also to wait for permits from the wartime prices and trade board, et cetera, et cetera. We are not free to export what we have. There are so many controls that the Canadian producer, the Canadian manufacturer, or the Canadian exporter is not free to trade with other nations, while the trade of other nations is made the easier. There are so many entanglements here that it is most difficult for any Canadian producer to ship his produce abroad to any other country in the world.
The first consideration in regard to trade being economic independence, the second is that we should sell at world prices; and of course it is not done in that way, because we sell at prices which are established by agreements. The Minister of Finance, on May 6, at page 1228-9 of Hansard, gave information about subsidies that are paid: For wheat flour, $147,000,000; fisheries products, $12,000,000; meat, eggs and cheese, $130,000,000, or a total of $273,005,422. It has been paid in part by a balance of $160,236,000 owing to the United Kingdom for the- maintenance of Canadian troops in the United Kingdom and in theatres of operation between April 1, 1943, and February 28, 1945. I will not say now what I think of the controls at present. I will not say all I think of them, but I say that it is wrong, and I regret very much the inferiority complex of all the men in charge of public affairs, their inferiority complex toward graduates of Oxford, Cambridge and other universities. I find we need the least possible number of those men in all departments, including the Department of Trade and Commerce. What we need is men of experience and business standing like the minister him-helf, but his aides should be equal to himself.
We hear a good deal about the scarcity of wheat in England and it is very strange, but I always have something vp my sleeve to
Supply-Trade and Commerce

establish the veracity of what I say. We are told they have no flour in England, and yet I have here the third letter that was sent to Mr. Emile Ouellette, a grocer of Riviere du Loup, by Peek Frean's Company Limited of London. It is impossible to get Canadian biscuits in any store here. One may get only a package at a time, and yet this is the third letter from Peek Frean's Biscuits to Mr. Ouellette. It is dated June 10, 1946 and reads: Dear Sirs,
We beg to refer to our export price-list dated February 1946, and have to inform you that, as a result of the increased cost of ingredients and manufacture, we have found it necessary to adjust the price of our Vita-Weat (Regd.) Crispbread in order to maintain the high standard of this product.
All orders dated as from to-day, therefore, will be subject to the net prices shown below.
How is it, if flour is so scarce over there, they can send us biscuits made in England when we cannot get Canadian biscuits over here? As regards the wheat business, I do not know what will be the understanding in connection with world agreements compared with British agreements, but in the United States the price of wheat is $2.10 and at Fort William $1.55, or a difference of fifty-five cents. On daily shipments of a million bushels the loss to the Canadian farmer is $550,000, or a loss over 300 days of $165,000,000. There was a subsidy of $14,300,000 to the wheat pool. It is a little more this year.
The London surplus wheat, mostly Canadian, was a million tons, and on United States pressure 200,000 tons has been shipped to the continent. It is exploitation. Why not follow the example of Peron, the President of the Argentine, who has exchanged amicable messages with Canada? The government in the Argentine bought all wheat at $5. It sold part of it to Peru for $9 and the other part to the Argentineans for $2, so that the exports paid for the cheap sales to the people living within the country. That is an admirable policy. Why, therefore, should we have the kind of policy on wheat that we have when there is a world price that we could get and get across the border, and get anywhere, and which the farmers do not receive? A huge amount is paid in subsidies for wheat, but the farmers are not satisfied because, even with those subsidies, they make a loss of $165,000,000 a year.

What was the subsidy on bacon and ham sent to Great Britain under Mutual Aid? What quantity did we ship to the United Kingdom in 1944, 1945 and 1946? What was the subsidy each year? Then, with regard to milk, what has been paid on the domestic production of milk? What quantity of powdered milk and cheese has been sent each year to the United Kingdom, and what has been the subsidy paid on it?
The reason why I do not agree with all the policies of the Department of Trade and Commerce is that we have built up a oneway trade with the United Kingdom at great sacrifice, and we are paying taxation for it. I do not see why we do not take advantage of the facilities that we have in this country to trade with other countries of the world.
I have other questions to ask the minister, but I should like to have a complete list of the subsidies which have been paid on food especially by the government so as to know what encouragement has been given to the export trade.
Before closing, I have only one more remark to make, namely, that the payments which are made to us are made from gifts and loans which we have made. It is most extraordinary, because our exports are paid for by taxation. When Mr. Bennett was in power I was interested in statistics on imports and exports, but at the time Canada was paying for her imports and our exports were paid for by the countries which received our goods. At the present time we are paying for both. We pay for the imports which come from the outside and we also pay by taxes for the exports that are made to other countries, because all the loans, Mutual Aid, et cetera, et cetera, come down to taxes. I sympathize with the minister; I mean it; I know of the obstacles he has in his way; I know the difficulties he has to surmount to reestablish Canadian trade as it was before.
We have great facilities to trade with other countries of the world, especially South America. To-day there are not many difficulties because we can practise barter; we can practise barter with all the countries of the world, and we should follow those trade practices. Great Britain indulges a lot in barter and they make a success of their trade. When we are told that we should have the trade of Great Britain it is forgotten that the trade of Great Britain is better now than it was before the war. Official statistics are to that effect, and the news has appeared in the press. It is not a question of not being a good Britisher
to say that Canada must go ahead and have the best possible trade as we had before. We have made gifts. It is time for us to think of ourselves and to give the greatest possible impulses to our own trade. I know that the minister understands me and I hope that he will be sympathetic to these suggestions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I certainly have no wish to hold up the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but I think it is fit and proper that I should make a brief statement on the estimates that we are asking the committee to approve.

speechtext:
I am not just sure which brief the hon. member for Peterborough West is referring to at the moment, but I can assure him-and I am sure he is aware of this -that the Department of Trade and Commerce works in close and helpful contact with the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. The work that the Department of Trade and Commerce is doing to-day for the manufacturers and producers of Canada is highly appreciated.
I should like to refer, for a moment, to the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo South. The import licensing system being operated by the United Kingdom authorities is basically dictated by their shortage of dollars and the need to devote their resources to the purchase of essentials. Early this year we were able to make arrangements which should ultimately lead to ensuring that those who have had a past history of trade with the United Kingdom will not be completely excluded from the market on the basis that their product is non-essential, but will be allowed to make at least token shipments pending the removal of import controls, to which objective the British as well as we are striving.
This arrangement for token shipments is beginning to work in respect of a limited list of commodities, and it is expected that the list will be extended from time to time. We are continually working on this matter with the United Kingdom authorities, but so far the United Kingdom does not include whiskies in the permitted list.
During this difficult transition period, and at least until the acceptance of principles which
Supply-Trade and Commerce

it is hoped will be adopted in the forthcoming trade talks, the choice as to how the United Kingdom will use its limited supply of dollars is, in the last analysis, a matter on which the United Kingdom insists on making the decision. Frankly, as long as bread is being rationed in the United Kingdom it is difficult for Canada to insist on any particular export to that country.
Before going into the details of the different votes for the Department of Trade and Commerce, I am glad to make a brief preliminary statement on the major activities which the Department has in hand, more especially on those activities which occasion the chief increases that I am asking the committee to approve in the estimates for the current year.
The aggregate increase in the estimates for the department runs into a substantial figure- roundly $3,175,000-and I should perhaps emphasize the fact that the responsibilities of the department are spread over a much wider field than, I believe, is generally appreciated.
Roughly, one-third of the total increase, or something over a million dollars, is required for the six divisions that make up the foreign trade service. Here, during the remainder of this fiscal year, we are going to have to meet heavy additional costs if we are to be in a position to provide all the facilities that are needed to prosecute our trade with other countries in the most effective way. The main additional costs are those connected with the ' extension of our trade commissioner offices abroad, and of our trade publicity programme, both in Canada and in other countries. We shall have to make added expenditures also, but on a lesser scale, in order to place our headquarters organization here at Ottawa on a basis that will ensure that we can give the most efficient support to the men who are carrying on trade promotion in the field. Since the close of hostilities, we have made good headway in reopening our offices abroad, but there is still p, great deal to be done in that direction before we can feel satisfied that we are adequately equipped to assist both import and export trade.
The heaviest increase in the votes for the current year, even larger than that for the foreign trade service, will be found in the estimates for the dominion bureau of statistics. Here the increase, compared with last year, amounts to roundly $1,360,000. Most of this is needed to cover the cost of the regular quinquennial census of the prairie provinces now being taken. However, there is a considerable increase also in connection with the bureau's general statistical work. This

is mainly to take care of new lines of statistical investigation which were initiated by the war departments during the war years and which are now to be continued-but only in so far as they are considered to be essential -by the dominion bureau. May I emphasize the fact that great care is being taken to continue permanently only those wartime statistical developments that are really indispensable to the work of one or other of the departments of the government. We have in the dominion bureau of statistics a national institution of which we may all well be proud. The demands that are made upon the bureau for the extension of statistical work are literally endless and unceasing. There is no such thing as finality in limiting the kind and scope of the work which the bureau has to undertake, but I am satisfied that the utmost care is being exercised by the senior officials at the bureau to see that new work is taken on and new expenditures incurred only in connection with national statistical needs that cannot be put aside except to the actual and serious detriment of the public or of one branch or another of the public service.
May I add just a brief further word with reference to three or four other sections of the department which call for relatively small increases in this year's appropriations, but which, nevertheless, discharge very large responsibilities?
The work carried on by the board of grain commissioners relating to the grading and inspection of grain and to the management of the government elevators is, in itself, an enormous business, one which affects in the most vital way the world-wide trade of this country in grain and grain products.
Again, we now have in the Department of Trade and Commerce the Canadian travel bureau. The work of this bureau during the next few years is bound to be of the utmost importance in rebuilding a type of trade, which I think everyone regards as one of the most promising avenues of Canadian commercial development for many years to come.
Further, we are now in process of reviving the Canadian government exhibition commission, which was dismantled and dormant during the war years. In the field of international exhibitions an active period lies immediately ahead of us. Within recent months Canada has received invitations to participate in numerous exhibitions and trade fairs abroad, and I am convinced that in a business way Canada has much to gain by getting a first-class exhibitions organization set up as quickly as possible. Attention is being given to that need.

Finally, I should mention a group of three services in the department which, although they are not much in the public eye, discharge duties of great importance to the buying public. These include the weights and measures inspection, the electricity and gas inspection and the administration of the Precious Metals Marking Act-all designed to protect the Canadian public over a wide range of their consumer purchases. Work of this type- inspection of scales, electric meters and so on -requires highly competent technical officers, and it is a class of work in which there is likely to be material expansion within the next few years.

Mr. MaeINNIS: I believe the hon. member for Waterloo South made some reference to the necessity of keeping costs of production down in order that we may get our due share of export trade. I have not the slightest doubt that representations will be made in that regard to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and that they will be supported by some manufacturers with a view to lower wages. But I would suggest to the minister that he consider carefully pleas of that kind, because they may not be all they claim to be.
Those of us who have been interested in political affairs for some time will remember that certain textile companies in the province of Quebec, late in 1935, or early in 1936, made representations to the present government, which had just been elected to office, urging increased protection on cotton goods because of the competition with Great Britain, and for increased protection on rayon because of competition with Japan; and they threatened that, if such protection were not given, their plants might be closed.
The government of the day, to its credit, did not accede to those demands, and appointed a royal commission to investigate. It is some little time since that royal commission made its report, but I would just suggest to hon. members that the report is well
worth reading, and particularly the brief presented by counsel appointed to assist the commissioner who, in this instance, was the Hon. Mr. Justice W. F. A. Turgeon. The counsel was Mr. J. C. McRuer, who at the present time is chief justice of the trial division of the supreme court of Ontario. Mr. McRuer began his brief with these striking, perhaps I might say startling, expressions:
A shameful, sickening, story of heartless exploitation and wholesale robbery by men prominent in the public life of Canada. Inordinate greed, barefaced lying and criminal fraud characterize the careers of this gang of high-class crooks.
These were the leaders in the cotton manufacturing industry. Their plea was that, because of foreign competition and what they considered the high wages they were paying to their employees, they could not meet that competition. But when the commission had made its investigations and completed its findings, it found, as revealed in the report, that the wages paid were less than those paid to coolie labour in China.
Another gentleman who held the position of associate counsel with Mr. McRuer said this, in his brief respecting competition:
It is destructive competition that maintains wages at a low level. When responsibility does not rest with foreign competition, it lies with domestic competition waged at the expense of the worker and resulting from the wage inequality between provinces, cities, towns and villages.
That is the statement made by Elie Beauregard, K.C., associate commission counsel at that time. So that I say the government and the minister should be particularly careful that they do not pay a great deal of regard to applications of this kind, and in any event, that such applications should be carefully investigated.
Export trade is important and, as I have said before in this chamber, the less selfsufficient a nation is, the fewer its resources, regardless of whether those resources are found in abundance or not. the greater is its need for export trade. But we need that trade, or we must have that trade as a necessity only in order that we may buy those things which we do not produce or cannot produce economically. Anything over and above that is trade that can and should be used to raise the standard of living of our own people. Let us be aware of the fact that Canada's best market should and must be in Canada itself.

speechtext: These items were put in at the time the estimates were being prepared, and the $10,000 is just a preliminary item.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: And it will be increased?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Item agreed to.
Dominion. Bureau of Statistics-
381. Statistics, including contribution of $2,530 to the Inter-American Statistical Institute, $2,090,670.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Does the compilation of the cost of living index come under this department through the bureau of statistics?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: There has been considerable criticism of the basis on which the cost of living index is prepared. It is desirable that we should have as reliable, a cost of living index as possible because it is used so often. I would suggest to the minister that he give consideration to having an investigation made of the items that should go into a modern cost of living index, with proper weight being given to the various items. The number of items included should, I think, be greatly increased to enable us to have a truer estimate of what the cost of living really is.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
There is a large increase here of nearly half a million dollars. We all believe in statistics and I have a high opinion of the head of the bureau; nevertheless it can run riot if there is no check. Who assumes responsibility for the size of the institution? It can be developed without limit unless there is someone keeping check on it. I do not

Item agreed to.
Mail subsidies and steamship subventions-
383. Administration, $18,333.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: When can the port of Prince Rupert expect the subsidy put back on steamships calling there?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The matter is under consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I wish to mention a matter of importance, namely, the ferry boat Kipawo which served in Minas basin, calling at the ports of Kingsport, Parrs-boro and Wolfville. There is one port in the constituency of Cumberland and there are two in the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings, represented by the Minister of Finance, who is not here to speak for his constituents. His constituents certainly need someone to speak for them in this matter. This boat was built in 1926 and named after the three towns involved, the ports of call. The boat was taken off early in the war and used for war purposes in Newfoundland. At the termination of the war it was sold in Newfoundland, even though the people interested agreed to invest a reasonable sum to purchase it or to secure a new boat to continue the service. During the war, motorists had to use gasoline and wear out their tires going 150 miles additional. This was the only ferry service in all Canada that was cancelled. I appreciate the attitude of the minister, because he told me personally that he was favourable to the continuance of it. The people have no service now. This ferry had been in operation for more than forty years. I would point out that unlimited sums were expended from the Canadian exchequer on the construction of ships of different kinds which have been sold at only a fraction of their cost. I have before me a list of some of these ships, but. I will not delay the committee by reading them. I will mention only two items among those brought before the war expenditures and economies committee. There was the Andre Dupre, length 125 feet; monthly rental, $1,187.50, cost 63260-3531
of repairs and rents while under R.C.N., $31,008.21; cost of reconditioning for return to owners, or cash settlement in lieu, $9,0.10.73. There is another one of which the cost of recondition amounts to $103,361.57. The people of the three ports were supported by the boards of trade in the ports of call and in the constituency of the Minister of Finance in order that this service which had been in operation for over forty years and which had always proved so useful might be restored. They have taken a great pride in the service. I would ask the minister to make a statement as to the policy of his department and its attitude toward securing a suitable ship and the question of having the service restored. If he takes steps to bring this about he will have the cooperation of all the people directly interested.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I remember very well the hon. member speaking along the same line with reference to this same service a year ago. Since then, to the best of my recollection, I have not had a single request from anyone for it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The boards of trade have taken action in an endeavour to get a vote.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I do not think anything has come to the department. However, I will look into the matter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The Kipawo was sold in Newfoundland under protest from the people concerned. They wanted it brought back.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I will look into the matter.

Item agreed to.
Canada Grain Act-
389. Canadian government elevators, including equipment, $740,923.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: What use does the government intend to make of the Prince Rupert grain elevator this year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: There is a great deal of wheat planned for shipment via the Pacific in this next crop year. I am not sure at the moment to what extent the Prince Rupert elevator is being used, but I shall make inquiries and write personally to the hon. member.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Could the minister make an additional statement in connection with Churchill facilities? There has been a good deal of discussion in the west, and he might indicate whether the Churchill elevator will be filled to capacity at the end of the grain season.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: I am informed that there is sufficient wheat at Churchill to fill the vessels which are already on their way to that port. I am further informed that the wheat board is providing from this crop sufficient wheat to fill at least two more vessels and to provide wheat for all ships that are being sent to Churchill. In addition to wheat, there are some other commodities that are being exported.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Will the elevator be filled at the end of the shipping season?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: With the situation in Europe we cannot promise to put any wheat in there that we shall not be able to move for a year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: It is better to have the grain there than in the fields.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: If we have a very large crop I can assure my hon. friend that the facilities at Churchill will be used.

390. To assist in promoting tourist business in Canada, $650,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Several provinces have travel bureaus. Does the department do anything to avoid overlapping?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: We have called a meeting of the various provincial departments that are in charge of tourist traffic. maintopic: SUPPLY-CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
As a matter of information, may I ask what the purpose is in making this motion now when there are still other resolutions to come?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am informed that the resolutions should be printed in Votes and Proceedings, and if we left them all to the last day it would leave too much work to be done on that occasion. If they are concurred in this evening the printing can be started at once, and this will facilitate the arrangement for final adoption of the bill based upon the resolutions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CONCURRENCE
speechtext:
The whole purpose is to avoid too large a bulk on some later matters?
